**Rhydia's overworld ace-bonding interactions — the two-ace structure `[LOCKED v0.9.8 — narrative; engineering OPEN]`:**

Per Section 11 — Ace-Bonding Overworld Interactions, Rhydia qualifies for the pattern with **two named aces deployed in parallel**, both present in her overworld appearances. This is the project's *original* two-ace structure (Section 11 — pattern); Ambrose Caymen (Temperance + Brunhilda) and Sable Ashland (Solara + Gouging Fire) follow this same pattern locked in v0.9.8.

- **Justice (shiny Iron Valiant, Sharpness ability) — the Champion-tier combat ace.** The royal heirloom Iron Valiant whose existence directly shapes Baradus's three-fears framework (Section 8 — Baradus's fears). Interaction tone: **earned-respect, slightly-formal partnership.** Justice is not Rhydia's pet; Justice is *the empire's living weapon entrusted to its Champion*, and Rhydia carries that weight visibly in how she addresses the Iron Valiant. Sample register: *"Justice, with me,"* *"Ready,"* — short, military-precise, *equal-partner* rather than commander-to-tool. **The interaction makes legible to the player that Rhydia respects the Iron Valiant's lineage and historical role**, not just its combat utility.
- **Puff (shiny Drampa, Multiscale ability) — the personal-companion ace.** Drampa is canonically a gentle, child-loving species; Rhydia's Puff is *visibly her personal partner* in a way Justice cannot quite be, since Justice carries the empire's weight. Interaction tone: **unguarded affection.** Rhydia is *visibly relaxed* around Puff in a way she rarely is around anyone or anything else. Sample register: *"Hello, sweetheart,"* a hand stroking Puff's mustache, a soft conversational murmur. **Puff is where Rhydia gets to be twenty years old again** — where the exhausted Queen-Regent / Champion can briefly *not* be either.
- **The two-ace contrast is itself character:** Rhydia carries empire-weight in her relationship with Justice; she gets to be a person in her relationship with Puff. **Both are real, both are the same Rhydia, both are necessary for her to survive what she carries.** Engaged players observe this contrast and understand more about Rhydia's exhaustion than she ever articulates aloud.
- **The relationship to Osrid's eventual return:** when Osrid is finally back in Rhydia's life as her brother, *Puff is the first member of the royal household Rhydia introduces him to.* Justice gets introduced through the Hall of Fame moment when Osrid sees Rhydia in combat at her Champion-tier; Puff gets a separate quieter introduction. **Puff is family-private; Justice is empire-public.** The distinction is part of how Rhydia signals to Osrid that she has *both* lives, and that her continued duty to the empire (Justice) does not exhaust her capacity to receive him as a brother (Puff).
- `[OPEN]` Specific overworld interaction beats — palace scenes, training-yard scenes (Justice), private gardens (Puff), the post-Osrid-reveal scene where Puff is introduced
- `[OPEN]` Whether Justice and Puff interact with each other in any overworld beats — recommendation: yes, occasionally; the contrast between the *living-weapon* Iron Valiant and the *gentle-giant* Drampa coexisting in Rhydia's household is one of the project's quietest character moments

### Gideon Valic — the previous Vizier of War (deceased) `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`

**Glaive's adoptive father; the Vizier of War assassinated ~1 year before the game.**

- **A peer of Prince-Consort Eldred Nightfall** and nearly his equal as a tactician — one of the empire's two great military minds. Northpoint-educated (Section 1 — Northpoint), of **House Valic.**
- **His grief, and Glaive:** Gideon lost his **wife and child** to a highway-robbery of their carriage gone horribly wrong. Years later he found an abandoned infant near the edge of his estate and, under extraordinary circumstances, took the child as his own — **Glaive Valic** (Section 7 — Glaive). The adoption was a bereaved man latching onto a second chance at fatherhood.
- **His death `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** **Baradus personally assassinated Gideon** roughly a year before the game, under "mysterious circumstances." It was a **targeted strike with two aims** — to further destabilize the empire, and to **elevate Silas Moray** into a more relied-upon, critical-operations Vizier role beyond mere commerce, deepening the Sword Cult's institutional reach through its asset. Baradus saw Gideon as a genuine long-term threat (an Eldred-tier tactician) and removed him as he had removed Eldred.
- **The two-stage decapitation:** with **Eldred (10 years pre-game)** and **Gideon (1 year pre-game)**, Baradus eliminated Cormoria's two foremost tacticians in sequence — Gideon having held the defensive line for the nine years after Eldred's fall. His murder is why the empire's tactical leadership sits at its weakest as the game opens, and why the seat passed to the young, grief-driven Glaive (Section 12 — Baradus; Section 6 — Eldred Nightfall).
- **Zeldra:** Gideon and **Zeldra Stone** (Section 7 — Zeldra Stone) were on poor terms in life, yet his death is precisely what set her on her independent cult-hunt — disliking the man did not stop his murder from troubling her.

### Glaive — Dragon Tamer, future Vizier of War, future Solomonar, future founder of Blackthorn City `[LOCKED — updated v0.9.7]`

**Origin — Glaive Valic, the foundling `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** Glaive was an **abandoned infant**, found — under extraordinary circumstances — near the edge of the estate of **Gideon Valic**, then Vizier of War (Section 7 — Gideon Valic). Grieving the wife and child he had lost, Gideon took the abandoned child as his own. So **Glaive carries the Valic name**, and though adopted he was **raised as a noble** and formally educated at the **Cormorian Northpoint Military Academy** (Section 1 — Northpoint), the empire's most prestigious academy and the alma mater of Eldred, Silas, Gideon, Cadmus, and Kimaris. *(The "extraordinary circumstances" attach to his innate, unrecognized dragon-empathic aura — below — not to any dragon bloodline: Glaive remains the first dragon-master without precedent.)*

**His vengeance — its source `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** the "residual vengeance" and "older wounds" that keep Glaive's heart closed (and Shelgon from evolving) are grief for **Gideon, assassinated by Baradus** about a year before the game. Glaive does not know the killer's identity and on some level **wrongly suspects Kanto and/or Johto** orchestrated it. His arc runs in three stages: **misaimed** vengeance (at foreign powers) → **correctly aimed** (he learns the truth — that Baradus killed Gideon — at the Wo-Chien retrieval at House Alban, Trial 6, where he encounters Baradus for the first time) → **released** (the partnership-defeat at the Vizier-of-War fight, the locked moment his heart opens and Salamence becomes possible). His eventual choice to make his home in **Johto** — the very region he once blamed — closes the wound. He ascends to **Vizier of War**, filling the seat Gideon's murder left empty.

**Critical background context `[UPDATED v0.9.7]`:** Dragons in our era are generally regarded in Cormoria as **the most wild and hostile Pokémon type to humans** — *and* they are *ecologically rare* in Cormoria because of centuries of suppression by the Tinkaton clan in the deep desert (Section 6 — Tinkatink Line Dragon-Slayer Bloodline; Section 2 — Solomonar title). The combined effect: very few Cormorians ever encounter wild dragons, and those who do struggle to master them. Some trainers across Cormorian history have managed to keep a single Dragon-type on their team here and there, but **no family has ever specialized in or mastered Dragon-types in the modern empire era**. **Glaive is the first trainer in 1700+ years of Cormorian history to be officially recognized as a true dragon-master — the second Solomonar in the empire's entire 2000-year span.** Cormoria publicly acknowledges that a *first* Solomonar existed in Cormor's third century (with a shiny Haxorus ace, identity forgotten to history), but Glaive is the first dragon-master since that ancient era.

He is described in-world as having something like "the spirit of a dragon himself or the aura of one." The truth, theorized by Vizier Umbra later in the game: **Glaive has an unrecognized psychic gift** — a *dragon-empathic* ability that lets him feel the emotions of dragons and dragon-egg-group Pokémon, and psychically communicate his own emotions to them. **He does not know this about himself.** No one else knows either, except Umbra (who theorizes but does not directly tell Glaive). It lets him bond with dragons naturally in a way most humans cannot.

This makes Glaive mythically singular. **He is the founder of a tradition that hasn't started yet** — the first Cormorian dragon-master in 1700+ years, the second Solomonar in the empire's entire history (Section 2 — Solomonar title). By the time of Dreamstone Mysteries ~2000 years later, dragons are tamed normally enough that there are Dragon-type institutions, gym leaders, etc. The dragon-mastery lineage *begins* with Glaive. His personal anomaly becomes humanity's eventual normal. **And the deeper-still truth (per v0.9.7):** the dragons Glaive masters are themselves the *survivors* of centuries of Tinkaton-clan suppression. He is not just the first modern Cormorian to master a difficult type; he is the first modern Cormorian to master a type whose rarity was *actively maintained by a hostile Pokemon bloodline* over the entirety of the empire's history.

**Glaive's wariness of the Tinkaton clan `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

Glaive does not hate the Tinkaton clan, but he is *wary* of them. His Sandaconda (Dragon egg group, Ground) is *literally listed* among the clan's primary prey (Section 6 — Tinkatink Line). His Salamence Blackthorn is the *exact* kind of apex-dragon the clan considers their hereditary enemy. His unease is *concrete and ecological*, not abstract:

- **If Osrid chose Frigibax as starter:** Glaive's locked v0.9.6 dialogue applies — extra respectful acknowledgment of the Frigibax as a fellow dragon (psychic-empathic recognition).
- **If Osrid chose Tinkatink as starter `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:** Glaive's in-battle dialogue with Osrid *changes slightly* to acknowledge the Tinkatink's heritage. **He does not hold the young Pokemon personally responsible** (the Tinkatink is a hatchling raised by Umbra, knows nothing of its clan), but his body language and word-choice signal that he *understands* what is in the prince's party. Specific dialogue lines `[OPEN]`.
- **If Osrid chose Teddiursa:** Glaive's dialogue is the neutral baseline — no Frigibax-recognition, no Tinkatink-wariness.

**The arc, in full `[RESTRUCTURED v0.9.8 — corrects v0.9.4 pre-game-Hermit framing; Hermit rescue is now an on-screen event between Glaive fights G2 and G3]`:**

1. The prince's childhood friend, from before the war
2. When Osrid is sent overseas as a teenager, Glaive stays in Cormoria
3. The cults spread false news of Osrid's death
4. Glaive, devastated and enraged, captures a **rare mutated shiny Bagon** — black and crimson coloring, very imposing. He names it **Blackthorn**.
5. **Glaive at game start `[CORRECTED v0.9.8]`:** When the player first meets Glaive at game start (G1, mid-Act-I), Glaive is **a fledgling Dragon Master** — a skilled Cormorian soldier with growing notoriety, lauded by Cormorian military peers for the rarity of his Bagon starter and his secondary acquisition of Turtonator. **His full dragon-mastery journey is *just beginning*** as the player encounters him; he has *not yet* received the Hermit's partnership-training (which the v0.9.4 framing erroneously placed pre-game). Glaive's full team across the game is built up *during* the on-screen story, fight by fight.
6. **The five Glaive fights across the early-to-mid-game `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`** — Glaive's character arc is told *through combat encounters*, with the player observing his evolution beat-by-beat through what he brings to each fight:
    - **G1 (mid-Act-I, beginning of game):** Glaive has only **Bagon (Blackthorn) and Turtonator**. He is angry, gaining notoriety, prideful. The player defeats him; he gets *madder* and storms off to build a better team.
    - **G2 (later in Act I):** Glaive returns with **higher-level Bagon (Blackthorn), Turtonator, and Scraggy**. The player defeats him again. **He tells the player he is heading to find "a true dragon in the desert"** — pursuing a legendary Garchomp. Then disappears.
    - **The desert sojourn — between G2 and G3 — is where the Hermit event occurs `[CORRECTED v0.9.8]`:** Glaive enters the desert pursuing the legendary Garchomp. He fails to acquire the Garchomp. He is **caught in a brutal sandstorm** that threatens his and Blackthorn's lives. **The Blue Moon Hermit (Section 7 — Blue Moon Hermit) rescues him from the sandstorm** and provides shelter for an extended recovery period. The Hermit gives Glaive **partnership-training** — this is *the critical event* of Glaive's early-game arc. The Hermit recognizes Glaive's psychic-empathic gift (Section 7 — Glaive's hidden psychic gift) and teaches him how to *deepen his understanding* with Blackthorn beyond the vengeance-fueled tool-mastery he had been pursuing. **The Hermit's partnership-training is what enables Blackthorn to evolve from Bagon to Shelgon.** Glaive also captures **Sandaconda** during this desert sojourn — *the dragon he met, not the legendary he chased.* **Sandaconda is the diagnosis of what the desert taught him.** The player is *not directly present* at the sandstorm or the Hermit's shelter; this part of the desert sojourn is *between scenes* and only later recounted to the player at the Trial 6 chapter onset (Section 14 — story spine; Section 7 — Glaive's recounting below).
    - **G3 (after the player wins Trial 3, Act I→Act II transition):** Glaive returns from the desert. **He seems calmer somehow** — more thoughtful, less angry. He tells the player *the desert changed him* and that he is *on a better path*, and that he needs to face the player again to look even deeper. **His team is now Shelgon (evolved Blackthorn), Sandaconda, Turtonator, and Scraggy holding Eviolite.** Player defeats him. **Post-battle dialog: *"Something is calling me. Let us meet again."*** He departs to follow an inner call he cannot yet articulate.
    - **G4 — same scene as G3 ending:** the "let us meet again" line is the G3 departure. The player does not see Glaive again until G5.
    - **G5 (before Trial 6, with Cadmus Umbra present):** Glaive is at the location where the player is making their way toward House Alban. **His team is now Sandaconda, Scrafty (Scraggy evolved), Turtonator, Dracovish, and Shelgon.** The acquisition of Dracovish between G3 and G5 is `[OPEN]` (possible Roma connection given the fossil-revival mechanic). Player defeats him. This is the fight that initiates the Hermit-revelation scene (Section 14 — story spine, Trial 6 chapter onset).
    - **The cooperative Trial 6 climax battle `[LOCKED v0.9.8]` (NOT a versus-Glaive fight):** At the *culmination* of the Trial 6 chapter — after the player defeats Indrid Alban and Wo-Chien devours him — Baradus and Sword cultists arrive, and **Glaive shows up to fight *alongside* the player** in a double battle vs two Sword cultists (his G5 roster, now AI-controlled as the player's ally). This is *cooperative*, not adversarial. **Glaive thus bookends the Trial 6 chapter: the G5 versus-fight at the onset (triggering the Hermit revelation), and this cooperative ally-battle at the climax.** See Section 7 — Indrid Alban; Section 14 — Trial 6 culmination; Section 14 engineering task #70.
7. **Glaive's evolution arc through the five fights:** the player observes Glaive's growth *via what he brings to combat.* The Sandaconda's presence at G3 signals the desert taught him about found-dragons over chased-dragons; the Shelgon's presence at G3 signals he received deep partnership-training; the Scrafty at G5 signals he has continued to invest in his existing partners. **By G5, he is no longer the angry prideful soldier the player first met.** *Show-don't-tell at its purest — Glaive's team composition is his character arc, visible without exposition.*
8. **Glaive is still ultimately driven by some residual vengeance after the desert** — *his heart has not yet fully opened*. The Bagon → Shelgon evolution is the *first step* toward the deeper bond enabled by the Hermit, not its completion. **Shelgon refuses to evolve further into Salamence** while Glaive remains pulled by his older wounds.
9. By the G5 fight, Glaive is regarded as Cormoria's only up-and-coming Dragon Master — a singular figure with no Cormorian precedent. The empire credits him for inventing dragon-mastery from nothing; **only Cadmus Umbra and the player (and Glaive himself) understand the deeper truth: the Hermit's recent partnership-training is what enabled the foundation Glaive has built on.** Most Cormorians do not know about the Hermit; Glaive does not discuss it openly outside the G5 scene.
10. When Glaive first meets the masked Rainhawk at G1, he does not recognize his lost friend.
11. **The prince reveals his identity to Glaive at the Vizier-of-War final fight `[CORRECTED v0.9.8 — was "mid-game major event"]`:** Glaive learns Osrid's true identity *only* at their final confrontation before the Champion fight, when Glaive is the Vizier of War with his full team (team `[OPEN]` — to be designed). **This is much later than the Bridget reveal (Trial 7) and later than the Rhydia reveal (post-Trial-2).** The full revelation order across the game: Cadmus Umbra (always knew) → Rhydia (post-Trial-2 assassination subplot) → Bridget Nightfall (Trial 7) → **Glaive (Vizier-of-War final fight).** `[OPEN]` the specific circumstances/mistake the revelation forestalls.
12. The revelation transforms Glaive — he begins to **truly open his heart** to his Shelgon. This completes the partnership-thesis arc the Hermit had begun *earlier in the on-screen game timeline*.
13. Off-screen between scenes, **Blackthorn evolves from Shelgon into a uniquely-shiny black-and-crimson Salamence**
14. Glaive ascends to **Vizier of War** — one of the four Viziers, fought by the player as a late-game gate before Rhydia
15. After the player defeats him, Glaive's heart is turned toward peace
16. He departs Cormoria, having heard of an ancient dragon-tribe in Johto living in harmony with nature
17. He becomes the first true Master and leader of that fledgling dragon tribe and founds a city in Johto
18. **`[LOCKED v0.9.9]`** **Wakahisa** — the exiled Johto shinobi (Section 7 — Wakahisa) — accompanies him home and becomes his partner after his Vizier-of-War defeat opens his heart; the implication is marriage. *Downstream implication, consistent with the lineage note below that connects Glaive's Johto dragon-line to Lance's family: their union places Wakahisa within that line.*
18. **The city is named after his Salamence — Blackthorn City**
19. Lance's family eventually descends from the Dragon's Den order Glaive establishes

**Glaive's introduction of the Blue Moon Hermit to the player and Umbra at G5 `[LOCKED — refined v0.9.8]`:**

At the Trial 6 chapter onset (after the player defeats Glaive in G5 with Cadmus Umbra present), **Glaive recounts to Umbra and the player the recent events of his desert sojourn** — *the sandstorm, the Hermit's rescue, the partnership-training, the Bagon→Shelgon evolution, and the lessons that have transformed him over the months since*. **This is Glaive describing a recent transformation, not a buried history.** His memory is vivid; his processing is ongoing; his willingness to share the story with Umbra signals trust the player has earned over the prior Glaive fights.

The conversation differs slightly by starter pick:
- **Teddiursa-pick:** Glaive notes that the Hermit *referred to himself with the phrase "Blue Moon"* — and Glaive *thinks there is a connection there* to the player's starter line. This is Glaive's pattern-matching from his own time with the Hermit.
- **Frigibax-pick or Tinkatink-pick:** Glaive brings up the Hermit as a possible *partnership-mentor figure* who might help the player understand how to bring the starter to its final form. (`[OPEN]` specific dialog connection points for each — recommend Mountain Gale-keyed for Frigibax and Gigaton Hammer-keyed for Tinkatink as parallel-but-distinct triggers.)

**Glaive's recounting (the G5 scene's content):** He explains to the player (and Umbra) that *during his recent desert sojourn pursuing the legendary Garchomp, he was caught in a sandstorm that nearly killed him and Blackthorn, and was saved by the Blue Moon Hermit*. The Hermit then *gave him partnership-training that helped him build a stronger understanding with Bagon*, which is what allowed it to evolve into Shelgon. **The Hermit also spoke of three moves "lost to time" — Mountain Gale, Blood Moon, and Gigaton Hammer — that he said are key to unlocking "the chosen partner of Cormor's Legacy."** Glaive openly admits he thought the old man was babbling in riddles at the time. **Only Umbra and Osrid catch the true meaning of the phrase — the player's starter is the chosen partner of Cormor's Legacy, and the three lost moves are what the player's ace needs to reach its final form.** Osrid asks Glaive where the Hermit is located; Glaive gives general directions; this initiates the Hermit quest (Section 14 — Trial 6 chapter onset).

**This is one of the few times Glaive openly discusses his recent formative transformation.** The fact that he is willing to share this story — even with Umbra present — suggests both the depth of his connection to the Hermit and his trust in the prince + Umbra by this point in the story.

**This connection has significant character-arc implications:**

- **Glaive received partnership-training from the same teacher who is *currently going to help the player.*** The Hermit is the *master partnership-mentor* of the project — Glaive is *the first* of his on-screen students; the player becomes the second. **The shared teacher creates a partnership-philosophy lineage that Glaive and the player both inhabit.**
- **Glaive's dragon-mastery has *Hermit-roots*.** Cormorian history will eventually credit Glaive as the first true dragon-master without precedent. But the deeper truth is that *the Hermit's recent partnership-training enabled the foundation Glaive is now building on*. **Cormoria's dragon-tradition is, at its root, downstream of the Hermit's teaching.** This connects Glaive's Johto-dragon-tradition lineage (and through it, Lance's family) *all the way back* to the Blue Moon Hermit's nomadic-tribe oral-tradition.
- **The Hermit recognized Glaive's psychic-empathic gift in the recent past, before Cadmus Umbra later does (during the on-screen game timeline).** The Hermit was a few months ahead of Cormoria's most learned scholar in seeing what Glaive actually was. This positions the Hermit as the *true expert* on partnership across species — not just a lunar-mystic recluse but the most experienced partnership-teacher in the world.

**Glaive's team composition philosophy (LOCKED):** Glaive uses the **Dragon egg group** philosophy rather than strict Dragon typing. Since no Cormorian family before him codified dragon mastery, he has had to *invent* dragon training from scratch through trial and error. He has learned that the *dragon spirit* manifests across the egg group, not just the typing. His roster (illustrative, not full team):
- **Bagon → Shelgon → Salamence (Blackthorn)** — his signature, raised from Bagon, uniquely shiny black-and-crimson
- **Sandaconda** — Ground type, Dragon egg group; defensively counters Ice (the canonical Dragon-counter)
- **Gyarados** — Water/Flying, Dragon egg group; Mega Gyarados presents draconically; covers Dragon weaknesses
- **Turtonator** — Fire/Dragon, legitimately a Dragon Pokemon. **Ruination buff `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`: HP 60→100, SpA 91→115, SpD 85→100 (BST 485→564); new ability Dragon's Maw** (×1.5 Dragon moves) alongside Shell Armor. The +40 HP turns its elite 135 Defense into a real wall (Shell Trap and Body Press finally function); Dragon's Maw + 115 SpA make its Dragon STAB a genuine nuke. Speed stays 36 — the slow anchor by design.
- **Sceptile** — Grass, Dragon egg group; resists Electric and Ground
- **Heliolisk** — Electric/Normal, Dragon egg group; Special attacker complementing his Physical-leaning core
- **Scrafty** — Dark/Fighting, Dragon egg group; immune to Psychic, resists Dark

**Frigibax-pick player special dialogue:** Glaive recognizes the *Frigibax* in the player's care as a fellow dragon — he gives extra respectful dialogue acknowledging the Frigibax. **The recognition is for the Frigibax, NOT for the player themselves.** The player does not share Glaive's psychic gift; Glaive is empathizing with the dragon-egg-group Pokémon in the player's party.

**The Blackthorn naming pattern:** The Salamence is named Blackthorn. The city is named after the Salamence. Glaive himself has no epithet — he is just Glaive, throughout. This is the worldbuilding hint: attentive players hear Glaive nickname his Bagon "Blackthorn" early in the game, and the city's name in Gen 2 lore takes on meaning in retrospect.

**Mega Salamence — acquired via the Baxcaliburite quest companion role `[LOCKED v0.9.3]`:**

Glaive's Salamence (Blackthorn) eventually obtains Mega Evolution capability. **In Frigibax-picker playthroughs, the acquisition happens during the post-Champion Ancient Cormoria side quest** (Section 6 — Baxcaliburite quest "The Origins of Cormoria's Dragons"):

- Glaive accompanies the player into Ancient Cormoria to seek "the origins of Cormoria's dragons"
- In a cave with a unique ice puzzle, the player and Glaive discover a special Mega Stone cache
- *Both* the Baxcaliburite (for the player's Baxcalibur) *and* the Salamencite (for Glaive's Salamence) emerge from this expedition
- The climactic battle is a 2v2 double battle: Mega Baxcalibur + Mega Salamence vs. Roaring Moon + Walking Wake (both level 120 Past Paradox dragons)
- *Glaive obtains Mega Salamence as a byproduct of this quest*

**The character resonance:** Glaive faces Roaring Moon — the *Past Paradox version of Salamence itself*. **The modern Cormorian dragon-master encounters the primordial form of his bonded Pokemon.** This confirms Glaive's bond with Blackthorn is part of a vast historical continuity stretching back to Ancient Cormoria. His dragon-tradition has *deep* roots.

`[OPEN]` Whether Glaive obtains Mega Salamence *only* through this Frigibax-picker quest, or whether he obtains it off-screen if the player chose a different starter. The simpler design is *Frigibax-picker-only* — meaning Frigibax-picker playthroughs uniquely produce the strongest possible Glaive across canon (a future bloodline-connection note about Lance possibly relating to this generational dragon-power continuity).

**Why this character matters:** Glaive's arc is the thematic thesis made literal. His Shelgon refuses to evolve while Glaive treats it as a weapon for vengeance. The moment Glaive opens his heart, evolution becomes possible. The player witnesses Pokémon-as-partners-not-weapons embodied in a single character. **And the deeper truth** — that Glaive's apparent talent is actually an unrecognized psychic gift his soul has been using to do partnership-work he didn't know he was doing — *underlines* the thesis: real bonds with Pokémon are quietly metaphysical even when the trainer doesn't notice.

**Glaive's Vizier-of-War final team — the apex dragon-master `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`.** His last stand before the Champion (cap ~90, with state Mega sanction). This is the heart-opened culmination of the G1–G5 journey — the partners the player watched him raise, now at their peak, plus the otherworldly capstone. Built on the **Dragon egg-group** philosophy, so the team answers its own weaknesses through kin rather than abandoning the theme.

| Pokémon | Type | Ability | Item | Moves | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Blackthorn** (Mega Salamence) | Dragon/Flying | Aerilate | Salamencite | Dragon Dance / Dual Wingbeat / Earthquake / Roost | Ace. The heart-opening payoff — one Dragon Dance off 145 Speed sweeps; Aerilate Dual Wingbeat is its STAB nuke |
| **Dracovish** | Water/Dragon | Strong Jaw | Choice Scarf | Fishious Rend / Crunch / Psychic Fangs / Ice Fang | Scarf guarantees it moves first, doubling Fishious Rend to a ~170-power Strong-Jaw nuke; Ice Fang answers opposing dragons |
| **Turtonator** (buffed) | Fire/Dragon | Dragon's Maw | Leftovers | Dragon Pulse / Flamethrower / Body Press / Shell Trap | The bulky anchor — 100/135/100 walls, Dragon's-Maw Dragon Pulse nukes, Shell Trap punishes physical attackers; resists Fairy |
| **Sandaconda** | Ground | Shed Skin | Leftovers | Stealth Rock / Glare / Earthquake / Coil | The glue/enabler — rocks, Glare paralysis (lets his hitters move first), EQ for Steel/Rock; counters Ice |
| **Sceptile** | Grass | Overgrow | Life Orb | Leaf Storm / Dragon Pulse / Focus Blast / Giga Drain | The coverage glue — resists Ground (cushions Turtonator's 4×), Water, and Electric; fast special breaker |
| **Naganadel** | Poison/Dragon | Beast Boost | Life Orb | Nasty Plot / Sludge Wave / Dragon Pulse / Fire Blast | The Ultra-Beast capstone *and* the Fairy answer — Sludge Wave punishes the type every other dragon fears; Beast Boost snowballs |

- **The Mega `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** the team Mega is **Mega Salamence** (Glaive has state Mega-Evolution sanction as Vizier of War). Gyarados is *not* in the final six — one Mega per battle, and Blackthorn's Mega is the whole point of his arc.
- **Naganadel — the across-universes wink `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** an Ultra Beast on a Cormorian dragon-master's apex team literalises Glaive's gift at its furthest reach — his dragon-empathy extends even to a dragon from *another universe*, a being no Cormorian could conceive of. And Poison/Dragon makes its Poison STAB the team's super-effective answer to **Fairy**, the one type the rest of his dragons fold to.

Fairy is answered offensively by Naganadel.

### Cadmus Umbra, the Pokémon Philosopher — Vizier of Education `[LOCKED]`

**Umbra is significantly more politically important than his Pokémon Philosopher title suggests. He is the architect of Osrid's protective exile, the keeper of the prince's identity secret across the entire decade between Eldred's assassination and the start of the game, *and* he has been Rhydia's personal tutor from infancy. He is the secret architect of the entire royal succession recovery plan.**

**`[v0.9.8 ADDITION]` Cadmus is also the *strategist* of the empire's covert Resistance Triad**, operating against both Ruin Cults from outside the official Concordance framework. The Triad's three members are **Cadmus Umbra (strategist), Nemo Korolev (operator — Section 7), and Falco Raptora (institutional-reach and senior counsel — Section 7).** Their existence is not known to the official Concordance; their operations are independent and not always coordinated; they share information when it serves and act independently otherwise. **Cadmus is the architect-mind of the Triad** — he is the one who maps the cult landscape, identifies pressure points, and theorizes the cosmological depth of what the cults are doing. *Players who notice the Triad's existence understand that Cormoria's visible leadership is not its actual defense against the cult crisis; the actual defense is three private individuals operating in the shadow of the visible structure.*

**`[v0.9.8 ADDITION]` Cadmus's lifelong friendship with Kimaris Langerin — and the deliberate compartmentalization:** Cadmus and **Kimaris Langerin** (1st Trial Baron / Reserve Champion / Langerin patriarch / Templar Arceus consultant; Section 7 — Kimaris) **grew up together at the academy** — they are roughly the same age and spent most of their youth in shared academic environments. The friendship has endured into adulthood and is one of Cadmus's most personally meaningful relationships. *Kimaris's reverence for Cadmus is near-fanatical — he considers Cadmus his intellectual idol and dearest friend, and would do anything Cadmus asked.* **And yet Cadmus deliberately compartmentalizes Kimaris out of the Triad's operational core**, treating him as an *adjacent* contact rather than an *inner* one. The reasoning is risk mitigation: Kimaris's institutional exposure (visible Trial Baron, Necropolis-keeper, Templar consultant, Reserve Champion, Langerin patriarch) makes him an extraordinarily high-value cult-compromise target. If Kimaris were captured, drugged, broken, or otherwise compromised, the Triad's existence would survive intact only if he never knew the operational specifics. **Kimaris does not know he is being compartmentalized.** Cadmus shares warmth, intellectual collaboration, and intel about *cult-infiltration-attempts-on-the-Necropolis* (which Kimaris is actively defending against and is the proper steward of) — but withholds Triad operational specifics, Nemo's deeper activities, and the strategic picture. **This is one of the deepest tensions in Cadmus's character** — protecting his oldest friend by keeping his oldest friend in the dark, out of love and the strategic necessity of the cult crisis. The same compartmentalization pattern applies to Cadmus's other individual contacts (Bridget Nightfall — Section 7); Cadmus keeps each adjacent contact separate from the others and from the Triad core, by design.

**Full name:** Cadmus Umbra. The cognomen "Cadmus" carries Greek-mythological resonance — Cadmus founded Thebes, brought the alphabet to Greece, and sowed the dragon's teeth from which warriors sprang. The educational-civilizational role tracks with his Vizier-of-Education portfolio. The dragon's-teeth motif resonates with Glaive's dragon-mastery arc — *Umbra is in some sense the seed-planter of the dragon tradition* (he gave Osrid his starter; Osrid's friend Glaive becomes Cormoria's first dragon-master). And *Cadmus is the man who taught warriors to fight by giving them the means* — which is exactly what Umbra did for Rhydia from babyhood.

**Public role:**
- Vizier of Education throughout the Cormorian Empire
- Empire-era equivalent of Professor Oak/Elm
- Ancestor of Professor Tenebris (Dreamstone Mysteries)
- Latin-shadow naming tradition (Umbra = "shadow"; Tenebris = "darkness") — deliberate family tradition
- Title "Pokémon Philosopher" rather than "Professor" reflects the pre-modern era
- A counterweight to Cormorian warrior-Pokémon culture — pushes back against weaponization-thinking even within the Empire's military traditions

**Rhydia's tutor from infancy `[LOCKED]`:**

This may be Umbra's most consequential single role. **He has tutored Rhydia personally since she was a baby.** Politics, battling, governance, philosophy, history, statesmanship — every aspect of his strategic capability has been poured into her over 20 years.

- He is essentially a *third parent* in Rhydia's life alongside Pierra (and Eldred, until his assassination)
- **Rhydia is in some sense Umbra's life work.** She is what he made when he had two decades to make her.
- His careful strategic mind is *embedded* in her thinking — she analyzes problems the way he taught her to, considers contingencies the way he taught her to, delegates the way he taught her to
- The empire's survival across the past decade traces almost entirely to his two-decade architecture of royal preservation: clandestine Osrid contact + daily Rhydia tutorship + own Vizier work + secret-keeping across all of it

**The hidden role re: Osrid:**
- **After Eldred's assassination 10 years before the game**, Umbra calculated that Osrid was the next assassination target as the last male heir. He **deliberately arranged Osrid's protective exile** — getting him out of the country under the cover of war service, judging that protecting Rhydia and Pierra was easier with Osrid removed from the country entirely.
- **Constructed the "Nomad Alban" cover identity** for Osrid using House Alban's quiet complicity (Section 2).
- **Maintained continuous clandestine contact with Osrid for the entire 10-year exile.** Communicated through some combination of Templar Arceus loyalist channels and other secret means.
- After Osrid was severely scarred in the Sevii Islands operation, **Umbra arranged Osrid's return to Cormoria** — bringing him home behind the Noh-styled Rainhawk mask.
- **In the first half of the game, Umbra remains the only person in Cormoria who knows Osrid is the prince.** Rhydia knows her brother is *alive* (Umbra told her years ago) but does not know he has *returned*. This is a deliberate Umbra calculation — *he is holding back the most personal information from his beloved pupil for strategic reasons.* The empire's safety requires Osrid's identity to remain concealed until the timing is right.

**The Umbra-Rhydia tension at the ~50% reveal:**

When Rhydia learns at ~50% through the game that "Rainhawk Alban" is her brother (during the joint Sword Cult encounter), **she realizes Umbra has been withholding this information from her** for the months Osrid has been back in Cormoria.

- Rhydia trusts Umbra more deeply than she trusts anyone else in her life. **He is the closest thing she has to a parent who is actually present.**
- *Umbra weighed his loyalty to the empire's strategic safety against his love for his pupil and chose the strategic calculus.* That is the kind of decision that haunts strategic geniuses — they make right decisions that injure the people they love.
- Rhydia *may* forgive him. She *may* not, at least not immediately. **Either way, the most trusting relationship in her life has now been complicated.** Umbra's strategic calculus has cost him something he cannot replace.

**The starter gift scene:**
- Gives the prince his first true Pokémon partner in the gift scene (Section 6)
- This is *not just* an inciting incident — it is **Umbra's deliberate bookending of Osrid's 10-year exile**. Boran Surge's "Pokemon as weapons" philosophy polluted Osrid's spirit for a decade; Umbra responds by giving him a *true partner* as the first thing he does on returning to Cormoria. **Umbra is consciously beginning Osrid's re-learning of partnership.**

**Strategic implications of Umbra's hidden role:**
- Umbra is one of the most strategically capable figures in the empire — possibly comparable to Eldred in his prime
- His scholarly exterior conceals a decade of strategic patience — protecting the prince by exiling him, then returning him when his concealment becomes more politically useful than his absence
- He earned his Vizier seat partly through this role as the loyal-keeper-of-royal-continuity during the empire's most vulnerable decade
- He is one of the four most influential figures in Cormoria *because* of what he has done quietly, not because of what he has done publicly

This is *not* a side quest — it is a **second main quest running in parallel to the Trial circuit across all of the game's 9 chapters.**

Nemo only learns of Osrid's involvement during the 9th Trial mutual recognition scene (Section 7 — Nemo). **The Umbra-Nemo-Osrid axis is held together by Umbra's coordination across two operatives who don't know each other's full role until the Trial circuit's climax.**

**The Umbra family Water specialty and the Jousteel line `[LOCKED v0.9.4]`:**

**House Umbra's noble-family Pokemon-type specialty is Water.** Water as the type of *reflection, depth, philosophy* — perfectly aligned with the Pokemon Philosopher identity. Water gives the family defensive coverage and access to the Steel/Fairy/Water meta the Cormorian aristocracy plays in.

**Cadmus Umbra's ace is Jousteel** (Water/Steel; see Section 9 — The Jousteel Line for full Pokemon data). Jousteel is *the* Pokemon species most closely identified with House Umbra — and uniquely so:

- **The Jousteel line is cultivated *exclusively* by the Umbra family.** No other Cormorian noble house, no commoner, no foreign trainer, no wild population has access to the Jousteel line. (Even Archbishop **Ambrose Caymen** once tried to coerce the family into surrendering a Joustroll egg — he coveted a Jousteel of his own; House Umbra refused. See Section 7 — Ambrose.)
- **The Jousteel line is the only known Pokemon species that exists *only* in Cormoria** (besides Keerin in legends).
- The line is *not* a singular individual ace passed down generationally — it is a *bred lineage* the Umbra family maintains as a family project. Each Umbra raises their own Joustroll → Jousteel partnership.
- Cadmus's specific Jousteel is his lifelong partner, raised from his Joustroll days. Their bond is *long-term family-tradition deep.*

**Implications for Cormorian Pokemon ecology:**
- The Umbra family's cultivation of this line is a centuries-old responsibility
- After Cormoria's eventual collapse, the line presumably ceases to exist anywhere in the modern Pokemon world *unless* descendants of the Umbra family (eventually Professor Tenebris of DM era) preserved seed-stock — `[OPEN]` whether this is canonical
- Rhydia, having been tutored by Cadmus from infancy, has spent her childhood *around* Jousteel — she may have her own quiet connection to the line; `[OPEN]` whether she has a Jousteel of her own (likely no — Umbra-exclusive cultivation is significant)

**The "three eggs" event in Cadmus's generation `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

The Umbra-family Jousteel-line cultivation normally proceeds at a cadence of **one egg per generation** — a Jousteel produces a single egg in its long lifespan, that egg hatches into a Joustroll, the next-generation Umbra head raises that Joustroll into adulthood, and the line continues. Centuries of disciplined husbandry.

**Cadmus's generation produced an exceptional event:** the previous Jousteel laid **three eggs instead of one**. Two of the three hatched within the Umbra household — one became the **overworld attendant Joustroll** seen accompanying Cadmus around his laboratory; the other grew into his **personal ace Jousteel**. The third egg remained unhatched and was **sealed in a deep cavern accessible only to the Umbra family.**

The third egg is the hook for the Trial 4 Joustroll Egg sidequest. Full Joustroll/Jousteel species lore lives in **Section 9 — The Joustroll/Jousteel Line**, including the canonical Pokedex descriptions, stat lines, learnsets, evolution chain, and the *Cormorian engineered-weapons twin-pair* narrative connecting House Umbra's cultivation to the broader Cormorian-engineering thematic. The Pokedex description for Joustroll itself is: *"A legendary species that serves the Umbra family. Their metallic bodies generate billows of steam as they race around."*

**Trial 4 Joustroll Egg sidequest — Cadmus's role `[LOCKED v0.9.8 — narrative; engineering OPEN]`:**

When the player reaches Trial 4, **a Water-type cult has taken over the deep cavern where Cadmus's family sealed the third egg.** Cadmus dispatches the player to retrieve the egg before the cult can despoil what no one outside House Umbra is meant to touch.

The cavern is held by a **Mega Gyarados boss** flanked by a **Crawdaunt-led clan of water Pokemon**. The player works through the cult's outer guard, solves environmental puzzles, defeats the boss, and reaches the **incubation shrine** where the sealed egg has rested across the generations.

At the egg-discovery beat, the player chooses one of two responses to the line *"Is it just me or is the egg glowing?"* — the choice gates whether the hatched Joustroll is shiny or normal. On return to Cadmus, his closing line: **"Maybe our Jousteels can even face off in battle one day! Wouldn't that be exciting?"**

**Narrative function:** the sidequest is the player's first direct participation in the Umbra cultivation tradition (previously discussed but never engaged with), and the moment where Cadmus's familial-philosophical warmth is most visible — he frames the player's hatched Joustroll as a *future partner-peer* to his own ace, not a tributary gift. The "exciting" line is one of Cadmus's warmest character beats in the entire game. The fact that the third egg was an *exceptional* event in his generation — not a routine third-of-three — means the gift is also a recognition of the player's specific worth to House Umbra's continuing tradition.

`[OPEN]` Whether Rhydia is aware of the third egg's existence prior to the sidequest. Most likely no — the third-egg event is family-internal, and Cadmus's *judgment* about who to entrust with its hatching is exactly the kind of careful strategic-pastoral choice that defines his character.

**What Cadmus Umbra knows about Cormorian deep history `[LOCKED v0.9.4]`:**

**Cadmus Umbra does NOT know the deep cosmological truth of Cormoria's founding.** Despite being the most learned scholar in Cormoria, despite being the Pokemon Philosopher, despite tutoring Rhydia from infancy — he carries only the *fairy-tale-level* version of the founding myth:

- He knows that *Cormor Dream-Eater fended off a great evil in the past alongside the legendary beast Keerin, and founded the nation from that event.*
- He treats this as *probably-true-but-uncertain* historical record — consistent with his philosophical character. An honest scholar acknowledges uncertainty about ancient history.
- **He does not know:**
  - That the "great evil" has a name (Phancero) or what it actually was (Arceus's shadow-self made manifest)
  - That Keerin was a celestial partner rather than a tool Cormor used
  - That Cormor was originally a vengeance-driven tribesman rather than a heroic brigand
  - That the Treasures of Ruin are inverted Dreamstones / Cormor's original sealing implements
  - That Missingno is Phancero's first incursion
  - That Arceus's non-intervention is *active mercy with limits*

**This is critical character framing.** Even the most learned scholar in Cormoria is *not* the lore-keeper of the deep cosmology. The Blue Moon Hermit is the *last* of the nomadic-tribe oral-tradition lineage that preserved the actual history. **Cormoria's institutional knowledge has lost the truth across centuries** — Cadmus has only the cultivated mythology, like every other Cormorian scholar.

**This makes the player's late-game Book of the Moon discovery *more* dramatic.** Engaged players learn things *Cadmus Umbra himself does not know* — they reach the deepest layer of cosmological understanding that exists in the world. **The Book of the Moon contains knowledge that Cormoria's most learned scholar would *want* to know but has no path to.** This is a powerful reward for the engaged player.

### Silas Moray — Vizier of Commerce, the tragic-redemption antagonist `[LOCKED]`

**Silas Moray is one of the most thematically rich characters in the project — a tragic-redemption arc that elevates him from "secondary antagonist with a function" to "twisted father-figure who completes his arc through his death."**

**Family identity:**
- Head of **House Moray** — Psychic-type master family, longstanding Cormorian military tradition
- House Moray and House Nightfall are *natural type-rivals* (Psychic vs Dark) and *political rivals* (both compete for military influence)
- Silas's family's specialty is *mind* — psychic types, telepathy, foresight. The honorable use of this gift is *truth-revealing*. **Silas's perversion of it is mind-control and memory-erasure** — the same gift turned to violation.

**The deepest original wound — Domdaniel's rejection in childhood `[LOCKED]`:**

Before the Pierra-love wound, before Baradus's corruption, before any of it — **Silas was rejected as a child by House Moray's generational ace, Domdaniel** (the shiny Scream Tail with Huge Power; Section 2 — Generational Aces).

In Cormorian noble tradition, the family's generational Pokemon bonds with the heir. **Silas, the eldest Moray of his generation, expected to inherit Domdaniel. Domdaniel refused him.** We do not know the specifics — perhaps Domdaniel sensed something in young Silas that became the man he is now, perhaps the rejection happened *before* Silas's own moral compromise and *caused* some of it. **The Pokemon's judgment, in any case, was that this child was not worthy.**

This rejection has shaped Silas's entire psychological landscape:
- **His relationship to power has always been complicated by exclusion from the family's deepest power.** He is Head of House Moray but cannot wield the family's strongest asset.
- **His psychic powers are his own**, built from scratch — Thauma (the shiny Hisuian Braviary) and Malamar are his constructed arsenal, not his inheritance. **Without Domdaniel, he had to build his own power from nothing.** His Vizier-tier capability is genuinely earned.
- **The rejection by his family's sacred Pokemon prepared him for everything else.** Being told he wasn't good enough by Domdaniel made the later cosmic injustices — Pierra choosing Eldred, Eldred's assassination, Baradus's manipulation — feel like *continuations of a pattern that started in his childhood.* He has spent his life trying to be *enough*. He never was, in Domdaniel's judgment.
- **He has *never* spoken openly about Domdaniel's rejection.** This is the kind of wound a Moray would carry in silence. The Moray family knows; nobody outside the family does.

**The thematic weight of Silas's eventual redemption:**

When Silas pledges true loyalty to Osrid after his Vizier defeat and unmasking (Section 10 — Act V), and when he dies in the sealing cataclysm psychically constraining Baradus (Section 10 — Sealing Cataclysm), **he dies redeeming Domdaniel's judgment.** The Pokemon said he wasn't enough; he proved Domdaniel wrong in his final act. **The rejection was earned at the time but no longer accurate by the end. Silas dies having become someone Domdaniel would have chosen.**

This is tragic in the most precise sense. **The redemption arrives moments before the cost is paid.** And it is possible that Brie Moray — the niece Domdaniel did choose — recognizes this transformation in her uncle before he dies. `[OPEN]` whether Brie has any scene with Silas's death.

**The unrequited-love wound (the *second* original injury):**

After the Domdaniel rejection (and built on its foundation):
- Silas, Eldred Nightfall, and Pierra were of the same generational cohort, all in or adjacent to court
- **Both Eldred and Silas loved Pierra.** Eldred *acted* on those feelings and won her. They married. They had Osrid and Rhydia. Silas watched from outside the family he wanted his whole adult life.
- This unrequited-love wound is the *next* layer of injury — Silas had already been told by his family's Pokemon that he wasn't worthy; now the woman he loved chose his rival too. **The pattern Domdaniel started, Pierra continued.** Eldred's success felt like another judgment against Silas: that he was, somehow, simply *not enough*.
- Silas's grief at Eldred's assassination was complicated, mixing genuine sorrow with the secret shame of relief mixed with the public shame of grief.

**The mental breakdown and recruitment:**
- 10 years ago, Eldred is assassinated by the proto-Sword Cult (orchestrated by Baradus)
- Silas, complicated grief overwhelming him, has a mental breakdown
- **Baradus approaches him with a lie**: the Beads of Ruin killed Eldred, and the Sword of Ruin is the only weapon capable of destroying the Beads and avenging Eldred
- Silas, broken and grieving, accepts. He becomes 2IC of the Sword Cult.
- **Baradus deliberately conceals his own role in Eldred's death.** Silas does not know he is serving the man who killed his rival.

**The double delusion (the real psychological architecture):**

Silas now lives inside two layered lies:
1. **First delusion (Baradus's lie):** "The Beads of Ruin killed Eldred. The Sword of Ruin will avenge him. I am avenging my rival."
2. **Second delusion (self-imposed, beneath the first):** "I am helping Pierra heal. I am lifting the burden of rule off the woman I love. My manipulation is *care*."

The second delusion is more dangerous than the first because it is *self-administered*. Baradus put the first lie in his head. The *second* lie Silas built himself — a private moral fiction that reframes his violations of Pierra's mind as *love*. This is how he sleeps at night. This is how he looks Pierra in the eye each day. **He does not see what he is doing because he has convinced himself it is the opposite of what he is doing.**

**The twisted father-figure dynamic:**

Silas has watched Osrid and Rhydia grow up *as Vizier of Commerce*. He has seen them at court functions, advised on their education, been at family meals. And privately, unconsciously, he has thought: *"in another life these could have been my children. I am the one who stayed. They are almost mine."*

This is delusional possessiveness, a category of unsettling that has no clean name — neither romantic nor parental nor adversarial, but a delusion compounded of all three. Silas has constructed a *phantom-parenthood* in his mind across two decades.

**Critically:** Silas's pseudo-parental projection onto Osrid and Rhydia is *never acted on overtly.* He doesn't claim them. He doesn't say it. **The audience reads it through his behavior and dialogue, but it is never named aloud.** This restraint preserves the *privacy* of his delusion and the integrity of the tragedy.

**Silas's military service and intelligence operations:**
- Served as a senior officer in two international Cormorian campaigns
- Fought alongside both Eldred Nightfall and Nemo Korolev — **Silas and Nemo were comrades-in-arms under Eldred's command**
- Currently controls much of Cormoria's intelligence apparatus through Vizier of Commerce position
- Uses his psychic memory-erasure powers as a *forensic tool* — erasing memories of compromising encounters from witnesses, intelligence officers, and other state figures
- The intelligence apparatus is *corrupted* through Silas. This is why Nemo Korolev built a *parallel* private mercenary intelligence network to hunt the cults — he could not trust the official channels.

**Silas's aces and his use of his psychic powers:**

**Thauma** — shiny Hisuian Braviary (Psychic/Flying)
- Name from Greek θαῦμα (*thauma*, meaning *wonder*, *marvel*, *miracle*)
- The fact that Silas calls his manipulation-bird "Wonder" reveals how he conceives of his power: as **thaumaturgy**, sacred and beautiful, not as violation
- Hisuian Braviary's canonical lore involves it diving from great heights with psychic-amplified shouts that stun prey. **Silas attacks from above and through the mind** — exactly his character.
- Mechanical role: high-tier psychic damage and manipulation in battle. **Battle kit `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`: Tinted Lens · Heavy-Duty Boots · Esper Wing / Oblivion Wing / Heat Wave / Roost.** Esper Wing's self-Speed boost fixes Thauma's mediocre base Speed; Tinted Lens drives Psychic through the Dark- and Steel-types that resist it (nothing is safe from *the wonder*); Oblivion Wing's 75% drain makes it a self-healing attacker that *also* answers Bug; Heat Wave melts Steel. (Oblivion Wing added per design v0.9.9 to make the bird *extra* dangerous.)
- Custom shiny palette planned (a more sinister color scheme to distinguish Silas's "perverted national bird" from the Templars' standard Braviary partners)
- See Section 14 (Production Discipline) for the pending custom shiny palette work for Thauma

**Malamar** — backup ace (Dark/Psychic)
- The Pokémon canonically associated with manipulation and control (Malamar's signature is Topsy-Turvy / Hypnosis-led psychological tactics)
- Likely runs sets focused on suppressive tactics: status conditions, stat-flipping, mental disruption

**Silas's full Vizier team — the mind-domination lock `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`.** Silas's gauntlet team (third of the four Viziers, cap ~90) is a mono-Psychic control engine built on a single idea: *he does not out-muscle you, he takes your turns away.* It traps the opponent in sleep and confusion, drains them while they cannot act, and sweeps the disabled husk — the truth-revealing psychic gift of House Moray turned to violation. Its two structural walls, **Dark and Bug**, are each answered several ways so the lock never has a safe exit.

| Slot | Pokémon | Type | Ability | Item | Moves | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ace | **Thauma** (shiny H-Braviary) | Psychic/Flying | Tinted Lens | Heavy-Duty Boots | Esper Wing / Oblivion Wing / Heat Wave / Roost | Self-accelerating, self-healing dual-STAB attacker; Tinted Lens pushes Psychic through Dark/Steel resists; Oblivion Wing answers Bug |
| Backup ace | **Malamar** | Dark/Psychic | Contrary | Leftovers | Superpower / Knock Off / Psycho Cut / Hypnosis | The Dark keystone — immune to Psychic, resists Dark/Ghost; Contrary Superpower snowballs through Dark and Steel; third sleep source |
| 3 | **Hypno** | Psychic | Insomnia | Wide Lens | Hypnosis / Confuse Ray / Dream Eater / Nightmare | The pure sleep/confusion/drain engine; Insomnia = the hypnotist cannot be slept; 115 SpD sponge |
| 4 | **Galarian Slowking** | Poison/Psychic | Regenerator | Black Sludge | Eerie Spell / Yawn / Confuse Ray / Slack Off | The unkillable disruptor — Yawn (reliable sleep), Eerie Spell (saps the foe's PP), Confuse Ray, self-heal; neutral to Bug |
| 5 | **Gallade** | Psychic/Fighting | Sharpness | Life Orb | Psycho Cut / Sacred Sword / Leaf Blade / Swords Dance | The punisher that breaks both walls at once — Fighting STAB hits Dark *and* Steel super-effectively; sets up on a disabled foe |
| 6 | **Hatterene** | Psychic/Fairy | Magic Bounce | Leftovers | Calm Mind / Psyshock / Dazzling Gleam / Draining Kiss | The manipulator who cannot be manipulated — Magic Bounce reflects status/Taunt/hazards; Fairy is the second hard Dark answer; self-healing wincon |

**The lock loop:** one of three sleep sources (Hypno's Hypnosis, Malamar's Hypnosis, G-Slowking's Yawn) puts the foe down → Nightmare and Dream Eater drain it while it sleeps → Confuse Ray (Hypno, G-Slowking) greets it on wake-up → Hatterene's Magic Bounce refuses any status the player fires back → Thauma, Gallade, and Malamar sweep whatever is left twitching. The player spends the fight unable to act while Silas feeds on them.

**Weakness coverage (the Dark/Bug problem, solved):** Dark is answered three ways — Malamar's typing and Superpower, Gallade's Fighting STAB, Hatterene's Fairy STAB; Bug by Thauma's Flying + Fire and G-Slowking's Poison-typed neutrality; Steel by Gallade, Thauma, and Malamar; Ghost by Malamar's Dark typing and Knock Off.

**Why a Galarian Slowking `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** the choice is *character.* Silas, whose whole life is shaped by an inferiority complex toward the major figures of Cormoria, watches Cadmus Umbra's Kantonian Slowking dismantle challengers in the gauntlet just ahead of him — and a man who has spent his life being told he is not *enough* reaches for the same power in its darker, poisoned form. He cannot have what the better man has, so he takes the corrupted version. It is the same psychology that built his self-made psychic arsenal after Domdaniel's rejection, and the same wound Baradus exploited. The roster echo with Umbra is deliberate — Silas measuring himself against a better man and coming up twisted.

**Silas's memory-erasure mechanics (limits):**
- **Short-term memory only** — hours to days, NOT core identity memories. Silas cannot erase someone's whole life or fundamental sense of self.
- **Requires reinforcement** — erasures fade under sufficient emotional reinforcement. This is why his Pierra-manipulation is *ongoing* and *daily* — he has to keep maintaining it, not set-and-forget.
- This limit also explains why Silas does not just erase Osrid's memories on first encounter. The cost-benefit isn't worth it for a brief encounter; only sustained presence allows manipulation to take hold.
- See Section 9 — Key Artifacts and Mechanics for the full mechanic note.

**Silas's hostility to the Beads Cult (driven by the lie):**
- Silas genuinely believes the Beads Cult killed Eldred (Baradus's planted lie)
- He is *actively hostile* to Beads Cult members, **including Eden** when their paths cross
- This creates dramatic tension when Eden's defection to Osrid's side puts her in proximity to Silas — Silas sees Eden as a member of the cult he hates, not as Osrid's ally
- `[OPEN]` Whether Eden and Silas have any direct confrontation scene

**The redemption arc (FULL):**

**The mid-game and late-game Silas beats:**

1. **Silas as Vizier of Commerce battle (one of the 4 Viziers)** — boss fight with Thauma and Malamar as aces
2. **After defeat, Osrid unmasks** — Silas's reaction-dialogue *implies* his pseudo-parental recognition without stating it (audience reads it, no character names it)
3. **Osrid/Umbra reveal the Baradus-killed-Eldred truth** — Silas learns that he has been serving the man who killed his rival and orchestrated the original wound that broke him
4. **Silas pledges true loyalty** to Osrid — not just because of the Baradus revelation, but because **the prince he privately considered his own son has come home and revealed himself to him.** In Silas's private cosmology, this is the moment he has been waiting for without knowing it. *The prodigal son has come home, and Silas, in his delusion, was always going to serve that boy when he returned.* This is the most coherent thing he has ever done.
5. **Silas serves Osrid through the final act** — likely providing intel on Baradus's operations, possibly helping locate Nemo's captivity (Section 7 — Nemo), possibly other operational support
6. **Final battle, Silas's death:** Silas uses his **psychic powers to constrain Baradus** and **destroy the resonance bond** that Chien-Pao is forcing on Baradus. The backlash of *destroying the resonance + the energy released as a byproduct of sealing all 4 Treasures at once is too much for humans to channel.* **Silas dies from the psychic backlash.** (Osrid loses his memories from the same overload — see Section 10 — Story Spine.)

**The thematic resolution of Silas's death:**
- His **psychic gift** (his family's hereditary specialty, which he abused with Pierra) is *redeemed by use* in service of protecting Cormoria
- His **service to Baradus** is reversed *in the same moment of action* — the man he served as 2IC, he now binds
- His **death** is the *cost* of using his power at maximum capacity
- **Pierra is still protected** by Silas's actions, but indirectly — by the sealing of the Treasures that would otherwise threaten everything, including her. **He dies enabling the protection his decades-long manipulation always claimed to be.** What was instrumentally a lie becomes literally true at the end. The shape of his redemption is the discovery that the role he played in delusion can finally be played for real.
- **Silas's death is the only uncoerced act of love he ever performed.** He couldn't be Pierra's husband; he couldn't be Osrid's father. So in his final moments he is both, briefly — protecting Pierra and serving Osrid simultaneously.
- Pierra survives the epilogue with Rhydia. The woman two men loved outlives them both.

### Ambrose Caymen — Archbishop of the Arceus Templar `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`

**The empire's top religious authority — a Steel-type master, a torn-three-ways man, and a recurring fight whose resolution moves him from paralysis to becoming one of Osrid's staunchest allies in the second half of the game.**

**Position:**
- **Archbishop of the Arceus Templar** — the top religious authority of the order that maintains Cormoria's civic-religious infrastructure (Section 4 — Templar Arceus Order)
- Sits at the apex of the order's **warrior-priest tradition** (the militant side of Arceus's service, alongside the civic-administration side that the Tavern network and Braviary travel represent)
- One of the four most senior religious figures in the empire alongside the Viziers, though the Archbishop's authority is *religious* rather than *political-military*
- Type specialty: **Steel** — completes the empire's institutional type-coverage map (Steel is otherwise unrepresented in formal Trial / Vizier structure, though ubiquitous in elite protagonist-side aces — Tinkaton, Justice, Jousteel)

**Team `[LOCKED v0.9.9 — full team]`:**

- **Temperance** — shiny **Kingambit** (Dark/Steel), primary ace. The name "Temperance" invokes the Christian cardinal virtue (self-restraint, moderation, balance). **A Dark-typed Pokemon as the Archbishop's ace is a layered statement** — possibly that *Arceus's order is willing to wield Dark as a tool in defense of the world*, possibly that *Ambrose himself carries some moral darkness* that complicates his public role. **Or both true at once** (this is consistent with the project's emotional register).
- **Brunhilda** — shiny female **Perrserker** (Steel), secondary ace. The name "Brunhilda" invokes the Norse Valkyrie warrior-maiden tradition (operatic Wagnerian resonance). **The Christian-virtue + Norse-warrior combination on his named aces is layered religious-cultural texture** — Ambrose's roster blends two different sacred-warrior iconographies. *The crusader-priest archetype emerges through the names alone.*
- **The full order — four cardinal virtues, two named warriors `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`.** The roster extends the naming creed: with Temperance already a cardinal virtue, the order's knights complete the set — **Prudence, Justice, Temperance, Fortitude** — flanked by the two named holy-warriors **Brunhilda** (Valkyrie) and **Roland** (the legendary Paladin lance-knight). The roster *is* the Templar creed, which sharpens the irony of the man fielding it (see the Umbra wrinkle below).

| Name | Pokémon | Type | Ability | Item | Moves | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Temperance** | Kingambit | Dark/Steel | Supreme Overlord | Black Glasses | Swords Dance / Kowtow Cleave / Iron Head / Sucker Punch | Ace — grows stronger for every fallen ally; the last knight standing, avenging the order. A leader *empowered by loss*, mirroring his hollowed-out order |
| **Brunhilda** | Perrserker | Steel | Tough Claws | Life Orb | Swords Dance / Iron Head / Close Combat / Crunch | The Valkyrie berserker |
| **Roland** | Escavalier | Bug/Steel | Overcoat | Leftovers | Swords Dance / Iron Head / Megahorn / Drill Run | The lance cavalier |
| **Justice** | Aegislash | Steel/Ghost | Stance Change | Weakness Policy | King's Shield / Sacred Sword / Shadow Sneak / Iron Head | The sword and shield — endures the blow (Weakness Policy), then strikes back twice as hard: combat as moral revelation |
| **Fortitude** | Corviknight | Flying/Steel | Mirror Armor | Leftovers | Bulk Up / Body Press / Brave Bird / Roost | The enduring armored knight; Ground immunity, reflects stat-drops |
| **Prudence** | Bronzong | Steel/Psychic | Heatproof | Leftovers | Stealth Rock / Body Press / Gyro Ball / Trick Room | The temple-bell relic — Fire wall, hazards, and Trick Room so the slow order strikes first |

- **Weakness coverage:** the three mono-Steel holes each get a dedicated knight — Ground → Fortitude/Corviknight (Flying immunity), Fighting → Justice/Aegislash (Ghost immunity), Fire → Prudence/Bronzong (Heatproof). Fire stays the team's softest point *by design* (Roland is 4× weak), which is thematically apt: the cults all wield Fire/Dark, so *heretical fire melts the holy steel* is the player's cleanest line of attack.
- **Trick Room (built-in, optional):** the order is deliberately slow (Escavalier base 20, Bronzong, Kingambit), so Prudence's Trick Room turns that into an edge — the patient knights moving out of time.
- **Fight placement:** second half, after Osrid foils the bishop-coup; **~L73–78** (upper-Trial / lower-Vizier), the moral-revelation single combat.

**The three forces pulling at Ambrose `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

Ambrose is not corrupted by the cults, but he is *not aligned with the crown* either. He has been paralyzed by indecision for years because three distinct forces pull him in different directions:

1. **Sword Cult pressure via Silas Moray:** Baradus, through Silas, has been pressuring and manipulating Templar order members for several years. **Some bishops under Ambrose's authority are secretly cult-aligned** and whisper conflicting information into his ear about imperial politics, the royal family's true motives, and the moral standing of the crown. Ambrose can no longer fully trust his own subordinates — and *that loss of trust in his immediate institutional family* is itself a form of cult damage.

2. **Genuine personal relationship with Cadmus Umbra:** Ambrose and Umbra are on **very good terms** through decades of religious-civil cooperation. Umbra has been candid with Ambrose about imperial matters within the bounds of state secrecy; Ambrose has provided religious-institutional support to Umbra's various initiatives. *This is a pull toward the crown.*

   **The hidden wrinkle in that friendship `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** the relationship is real, but it carries a wound — and the wound is Ambrose's. Years ago, **Ambrose tried to coerce the Umbra family into surrendering a Joustroll egg.** He coveted a Jousteel of his own — wanted, badly, the one Pokémon his friend possessed that no amount of Templar authority could grant him (the line is cultivated *exclusively* by House Umbra; see the Jousteel-line section). Cadmus refused, and quietly never forgot. **It is a core reason Cadmus does not *fully* confide in Ambrose** even now — his candor always stopping just short of total trust. The wrinkle is what makes Ambrose human and tragic: the Archbishop who names his knights for the cardinal virtues — *Temperance, Prudence* — carries the one vice he cannot master, **covetousness**, and he knows it is wrong even as the envy gnaws at him. **It also quietly binds him to Goma:** the Harbinger of the cult of *envy* and the Archbishop of the holy order are, beneath everything, running on the same engine — one wearing it openly, the other strangling it behind a virtuous face. His Steel order's virtue-names are an act of self-discipline against his own envy as much as they are a creed.

3. **Deep formative friendship with Nemo Korolev:** When Nemo arrived in Cormoria as a Sinnohian war-orphan and grew up in and around the Templar order, **he became close friends with the young Ambrose.** The friendship persisted into adulthood — even as Nemo rose to Dawnstar and then stepped down to the 9th Trial Baron seat, even as Ambrose rose to Archbishop, they remained close adult friends across decades. **Of all Ambrose's relationships, this is the deepest.** *And this is the pull that Silas's lie targets.*

**The Silas lie about Nemo `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

At some point in the early-to-mid game, **Silas — under Baradus's orders — tells Ambrose a calculated lie about Nemo's career:** that *"Nemo was forced to become a Trial Baron by the crown as punishment for rejecting the empire's demands that he commit atrocities overseas for the Cormorian military."*

**The truth (already locked Section 7 — Nemo):** Nemo *voluntarily* stepped down from Dawnstar to negotiate the 9th Trial Baron seat himself, in exchange for the operational obscurity he needed to run his private cult-hunting intelligence network.

**The lie's psychology — surgical precision targeting Ambrose's vulnerabilities:**
- The lie frames the *crown* as the aggressor against Nemo (Ambrose's beloved friend) — which is the *one* claim that could turn the Archbishop against Pierra and Rhydia
- It positions Nemo as the *moral hero* who refused atrocities, which is *fully consistent with Ambrose's existing view of his friend* (Nemo is the kind of man who would refuse atrocities)
- It exploits Ambrose's *love for Nemo* to turn that love into anti-crown sentiment
- **Silas can deliver this credibly because Silas served alongside Nemo under Eldred for years.** The man telling the lie has the documented military relationship with the supposed victim that makes the lie *plausible*

**Silas's calculation is masterful and the cruelest specific act of his cult-aligned career.** He served beside Nemo. They were comrades-in-arms. Silas knows the truth about Nemo's voluntary retirement deal (he was Vizier of Commerce during the negotiation, part of the apparatus). **And Silas chose to weaponize that knowledge to corrupt Nemo's other closest friend.**

**Holding a Mega-Dreamstone shard `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

Ambrose secretly possesses **one of the 9 scattered Mega-Dreamstone shards** (Section 9 — The Mega-Dreamstone Shard Quest). He has been holding it for years, unsure whom to entrust it to:

- The crown might use it to consolidate power *or* might fail to protect it from the cults
- The cults are after it but Ambrose understands them well enough to know they would weaponize it
- The Templar order itself contains cult-aligned bishops Ambrose cannot trust
- **There is no one Ambrose can fully trust.** And so he holds it himself, alone, and the holding is eating him alive.

**He is in near emotional hysteria internally** — though he holds it together publicly because an Archbishop visibly hysterical would precipitate a political crisis. The shard's weight (literal and figurative) is *compounding* his torn-three-ways indecision. *He cannot give it to the wrong side, and he cannot identify the right side.*

**The fight context — the bishop-coup foil `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

In the second half of the game, the **cult-aligned bishops under Ambrose's authority attempt a coup** — they move to seize the Templar apparatus from Ambrose, which would deliver empire-wide religious-civic infrastructure to the Sword Cult (the Tavern network, the Braviary travel system, the order's intelligence-gathering, the institutional moral authority). **Osrid intervenes and foils the coup, fighting off the cult-aligned bishops.**

At that moment, Ambrose — who has been paralyzed by indecision for years — decides that he needs to **fight Osrid himself** as the way to *"get to the truth of things."* His coping mechanism for years of paralysis becomes a single-combat moral test:

**For a Templar of the Arceus order — whose entire theology rests on partnership as cosmic-sacred — combat is a form of moral revelation.** Ambrose cannot tell through political argument who is telling him the truth. But he *can* judge a man through how that man fights and bonds with his Pokemon. **Ambrose is using the Pokemon-as-truth framework to break his own paralysis.**

**The fight itself:**
- Player team vs. Ambrose `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`: the full Steel order — Temperance (Kingambit) / Brunhilda (Perrserker) / Roland (Escavalier) / Justice (Aegislash) / Fortitude (Corviknight) / Prudence (Bronzong).
- Combat tier `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`: second-half placement after the bishop-coup is foiled — **~L73–78** (upper-Trial / lower-Vizier).
- **The fight is a moral revelation event for Ambrose, not a strategic obstacle for Osrid.** The combat is *real and difficult*, but its narrative purpose is *Ambrose's clarity*, not the player's progression

**The resolution — clarity and alliance `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

Once Osrid defeats Ambrose, **Ambrose gains true clarity.** The partnership demonstrated in combat communicates a moral truth that political argument could not. **Ambrose:**

- **Surrenders the Mega-Dreamstone shard to Osrid** — joining the shard collection toward the eventual cosmological resolution
- **Begins the process of cleansing cult influence out of the Templar order** — purging the corrupted bishops, restoring the order's institutional health
- **Eventually learns that Silas's "Nemo punishment" story was a lie** (likely after Silas's death and the truth-revelation cascade that follows). *The grief of having been manipulated using Nemo's name is one of the most painful character beats in Ambrose's arc.* `[OPEN]` whether Ambrose explicitly forgives Silas posthumously or carries the betrayal with him
- **Becomes one of Osrid's staunchest allies into the final half of the game**

**Necropolis Assault — named defender `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

**`[v0.9.8 ADDITION]` Ambrose's long-running consultancy with Kimaris Langerin:** The Archbishop regularly calls on **Kimaris Langerin** (1st Trial Baron / Langerin patriarch / Reserve Champion; Section 7 — Kimaris) and the Langerin family's top mediums to handle hauntings and supernatural phenomena that the lesser Templar priests cannot resolve. This is an *ongoing institutional relationship*, not ad-hoc — the Templar order's spiritual-affairs department has a *standing referral* relationship with House Langerin. The relationship long predates the late-game Necropolis Assault (below); when Ambrose and Kimaris fight side-by-side at the climactic Sword Cult incursion, it is the late-game escalation of years of institutional alliance. **The relationship situates Ambrose, Kimaris, and the Templar order in a three-way infrastructure web** (Section 12 — Five-Oldest-Houses): House Raptora engineered the Braviary mount system; the Templar order operationalizes it + the empire's daily religious-civic infrastructure; House Langerin handles the supernatural-affairs consultancy for problems beyond the lesser priests' capability. *Three old institutions, three complementary specialties, one woven empire.*

Ambrose fights alongside the player at the Necropolis Assault (Section 10 — Act VI) as a named defender, deploying Temperance and Brunhilda against the Sword Cult's incursion. **He is one of the major institutional figures the player can count on in the climactic operation** alongside Kimaris (with Marshadow), Brie (with Domdaniel), House Langerin retainers, and the broader Templar Arceus order operatives. **The Archbishop's presence at the Necropolis is also the Templar order's *public commitment* against the cults** — a religious-institutional declaration that the cults have no friend in Arceus's house.

**Why Ambrose matters thematically:**

Ambrose joins **Silas (corrupted, redeemed in death) and Glaive (vengeful, opened by partnership-teaching)** as the third major institutional figure whose moral arc resolves through *being defeated by Osrid in a Pokemon battle* and *gaining clarity through that defeat.* **All three arcs use the same mechanism: Osrid wins a Pokemon battle against a confused institutional figure, and the partnership demonstration communicates a moral truth that political argument couldn't.** This is the partnership thesis weaponized at the institutional scale — Osrid doesn't just save Cormoria from cults; he saves three major institutional figures from their respective forms of moral confusion, and he does it by *winning Pokemon battles against them.* (See Section 11 — Design Principles for the three-redemption-arc-pattern note.)
