| 4 | Primarina | Liquid Voice | Throat Spray | Calm Mind / Moonblast / Hyper Voice / Psychic |
| 5 | Granbull | Intimidate | Leftovers | Play Rough / Close Combat / Fire Fang / Bulk Up |
| 6 | Whimsicott | Prankster | Focus Sash | Tailwind / Encore / Taunt / Moonblast |

  - **Strategy:** Whimsicott is the engine — Prankster-priority **Tailwind** flips the team's whole speed tier, or **Encore/Taunt** neutralizes the player's lead. Then a four-breaker assault: two Huge Power *physical* hammers (Domdaniel — fast, bulky, Wish-sustained; Mega Mawile with Sucker Punch priority) and two *special* setup sweepers (Togekiss Nasty Plot, Primarina Calm Mind). The anti-Fairy walls are pre-answered — **Steel** falls to Granbull's Close Combat, Togekiss's Flamethrower, and Primarina's Water-typed Hyper Voice (Liquid Voice); **Poison** falls to Primarina's and Domdaniel's Psychic moves. Granbull's Intimidate cushions physical hits. Bringing the obvious Steel/Poison counter doesn't save the player — that is where the +15 spike lives.
  - **Tinkaton excluded by design `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** Tinkaton is one of the three player starters (the Fairy/Steel dragon-slayer line) and tied to the Tinkaton-clan ecology and the Solomonar lore; a Trial Baroness cannot field the player's own starter-species. Mega Mawile fills the Fairy/Steel niche instead.
- **Trial 8 victory grants the Glamour Badge `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`** — "glamour," the old word for fae enchantment: pure Fairy, with a youthful sparkle fitting a 15-year-old prodigy.
- **Pre-battle dialogue from Brie:** she tells the player directly about her concerns with her uncle. *She does not soften it for political reasons.* The player will hear a 15-year-old speak the truth about a Vizier in front of the prince. This is one of the most morally clear-eyed dialogue beats in the game.
- **Post-battle dialogue from Brie:** depending on victory `[OPEN]`, may include her acknowledging that the player needs to confront her uncle directly and offering whatever help she can give

**Silas's reaction to Brie holding a Trial Baroness seat `[OPEN]`:**

Silas's *public* reaction is presumably proud — supporting the family's youngest as a public face of House Moray is politically obligatory. His *private* feelings are far more complicated. Possibilities (any combination):
- Bitter that Domdaniel's choice has been formally publicly ratified
- Quietly proud despite himself — he raised her, and her accomplishment is partly *his* parenting
- Threatened by her growing power — she is now the family member with formal political standing other than himself
- *Worried for her* — he knows what he's involved with, and a Brie with formal political visibility is a *target* in ways the cult-protected family-private Brie was not

The bible leaves this `[OPEN]` for future design but the dramatic possibilities are rich.

**Brie's later story arc:**

The v0.9.6 bible's open possibilities for Brie remain — she may:
- Participate in the Necropolis Assault as part of the multi-house defensive convergence (now *almost certain* given her Trial Baroness status; combat tier matches)
- Witness or be present at Silas's death in the sealing cataclysm — *the loss is double*: the father-figure she remembers loving as a small child *and* the corrupted man she has been fighting against in her own quiet way for years. **Both deaths arrive in the same moment.** This is one of the most emotionally weighted possible scenes in the project; treatment `[OPEN]`
- Become formal head of House Moray after Silas's death — at 15-16, the youngest noble succession in recent memory

**Why Brie matters thematically:**

She is the *family's hope* in a story full of family-failure: Pierra cannot protect her children; Silas corrupted his own house; the Ashlands lost Sable for 10 years; the Surge family raised a son whose worldview ruined another man's son. **Brie is the *next generation* the project promises will be different.** Domdaniel chose her *because* she represents the possibility of a Moray-future that isn't broken. **And the relationship with Silas — love and grief and rebellion and complicity all coexisting in a single teenage girl's heart — is the project's tightest demonstration of permanent emotional complexity (Section 11 Principle 2).**

**Combat profile:**
- At 15, Brie is presumably not yet at full noble-trainer power, but she has Domdaniel
- Domdaniel itself is Champion-tier (Section 9 — Domdaniel combat profile)
- **In Brie's hands, Domdaniel is constrained by her age and inexperience** — she may not deploy the Pokemon at maximum capability yet, the way Rhydia deploys Justice
- However, even partial use of Domdaniel makes Brie one of the strongest young trainers in Cormoria; her Trial Baroness seat is *earned*, not ceremonial

### Nemo Korolev — 9th Trial Baron, "The Usurper" `[LOCKED]`

**One of the deepest characters in the project. The Trial Baron who is also the secret destroyer of the Vessels of Ruin cult. Killed by Baradus in the late game, his death drives Osrid's commitment to becoming Champion + Regent-King and confronting the cults directly.**

**`[v0.9.8 ADDITION]` Nemo is also the *operator* of the empire's covert Resistance Triad**, alongside Cadmus Umbra (strategist) and Falco Raptora (institutional-reach senior counsel). The Triad operates against both Ruin Cults outside the official Concordance framework. **Nemo is the one who *acts most directly*** — his killing of Harbinger Alaric and his ongoing containment of Ting-Lu are the Triad's most consequential operational moves. He works alone in the field; he reports out to the other two; the three coordinate where possible and respect each other's independent judgment otherwise. **The Triad's existence is one of the project's quietest political truths**, never spoken aloud in the empire's visible institutions, only inferred by engaged players from small consistent observations across the late-game story.

**Origin: Sinnohian war orphan.**
- Was a child soldier in Sinnoh, already deployed in combat before legal enlistment age
- Taken in by a **Cormorian military-managed orphanage** (Section 2) after a Cormoria-Sinnoh territorial dispute ~30 years before the story
- Drafted formally into the Cormorian military as a teenager
- Rose through the ranks rapidly, by merit alone

**Military career — singular in Cormorian history:**
- **Arguably the single most talented and accomplished military officer in Cormoria's entire history.**
- Reached **Rainhawk** rank — earned through field promotion (the same rank Osrid earned)
- Served as a senior officer under **both Eldred Nightfall and Silas Moray** in two international campaigns. **He and Silas were comrades-in-arms.** (This becomes critical: Baradus deliberately hides Nemo's identity from Silas, knowing that even loyal-Silas would emotionally conflict if he knew Nemo was the Usurper.)
- Promoted to **Tarasque**, then to **Dawnstar** — highest military rank, equivalent of a Japanese shogun
- **Rose to Dawnstar faster than Eldred Nightfall ever did.** This is a remarkable fact considering Eldred himself was an exceptional officer who became Prince-Consort.
- That is a *meritocratic peak* for a non-noble, non-Cormorian-born orphan. **Nemo maxed the entire Cormorian military hierarchy without family connections, faster than anyone in living memory.** He is the empire's best living argument for its own meritocratic values.
- His ascent passed through every prestige tier (Windshear, Rainhawk, Tarasque, Dawnstar) without any noble birth or political protection. He may well be the first non-Cormorian-born Dawnstar in the empire's history.

**The surname exception — a unique theological singularity (Section 2):**
- The standard Cormorian custom: knighting a Rainhawk into nobility = bestowing a new Arceus-blessed surname on them
- Nemo *forfeited* the offer to be knighted (and the new Cormorian House surname that would have come with it)
- In exchange, he negotiated to **retain his Sinnohian birth surname "Korolev"** — with formal recognition from the Empress Pierra and the Viziers
- **This is the only known case in Cormorian history of a non-royal-bestowed surname being acknowledged as legitimate by the Cormorian state.** It is a *theological* anomaly, not just a political one (see Section 2 — Cormorian surnames and the divine right of naming).
- Nemo could have founded a new Cormorian noble house — the Korolev House, with its own type tradition and Trial Baron seat in due time. He gave that up to preserve his Sinnohian identity.
- More conservative noble families *quietly resent* this exception.

**The secret savior — Nemo's true historical significance `[LOCKED]`:**

In addition to being the empire's most talented military officer, **Nemo is arguably the most consequential individual in Cormoria's recent history in terms of what he prevented.**

Consider the counterfactual: had Nemo *not* intercepted Ting-Lu from Harbinger Alaric ~2 years before story start:
- **Baradus would have had access to Ting-Lu** (probably through ambushing Alaric himself, the same way he ambushed the Tablets Cult to seize Wo-Chien)
- The Sword Cult would have held *two* Treasures — Wo-Chien (from Tablets Cult slaughter) and Ting-Lu (from Vessels Cult capture)
- With two Treasures + 10 years of Silas-corruption-of-Pierra + cult infiltration of the Concordance and Templars + Sylphon & Stone funding the Beads Cult's parallel operations + the *time* gained by not having to track an unknown "Usurper" — **the cults would have taken over Cormoria long before Osrid was forced to return.**

**Nemo's single act — stealing Ting-Lu from under the cults' noses — was the act that delayed the cult takeover of Cormoria by 2+ critical years.** Enough time for Osrid to grow up overseas, for Rhydia to mature into her solo regency, for the protagonist's return to be possible. **He bought the empire its salvation window.**

**He does not know this.** Nemo's calculus when he killed Alaric was to neutralize a single cult and acquire a Treasure he believed he could safely contain. He could not have known that his action's downstream consequences included delaying an entire imperial collapse, enabling the prince's return, and preserving Cormoria for Osrid's eventual climactic confrontation with Baradus. **He is the secret savior who does not realize what he saved.**

**The full arc of the empire's salvation now traces through Nemo's two acts:**
1. **Stealing Ting-Lu** (2 years before story start) — buys the empire 2+ critical years
2. **Passing Ting-Lu to Osrid** (during his death scene) — enables the climactic sealing ritual

**Without either act, Cormoria would fall.** Without the first, the empire collapses before Osrid returns. Without the second, the climax has no Treasure capable of initiating the seal. **Nemo's two-act contribution — invisible to him at the time of each act — is structurally the foundation of the entire game's possibility.**

This recharacterization makes Nemo's death even more crushing. He says "*help the prince put an end to this*" — but the audience now understands that **Nemo has been helping prepare for this moment for 2+ years already, without knowing it.** His death is the *completion* of an arc that began with the Alaric ambush. He doesn't get to see what his actions enabled. He gives Ting-Lu to Osrid and dies. The empire owes him its existence and never publicly acknowledges this fact — Cormorian historians may eventually piece it together, but at the moment of his death, **only the player and reader understand what Nemo really did.**

**Idolized Eldred. Devastated by his assassination.**
- Eldred Nightfall represented "the ideal leader" to Nemo
- Eldred's assassination 10 years ago shattered Nemo's faith in the system he had spent his life rising through. The empire that he served could not protect its own prince-consort. The system was vulnerable in ways he had not understood.
- **The grief did not paralyze him. It channeled him.** He decided to act outside the corrupted official channels.

**The Trial Baron negotiation:**
- After Eldred's assassination, Nemo voluntarily **vacated his Dawnstar position** — a profound and shocking decision in court
- Made a deal with the Viziers for the **9th Trial Baron seat** (Ground-type specialty)
- The seat was available because the prior Ground-type house, **House Jalviss**, had been destroyed in the Aerodactyl Mega Evolution accident (Section 2 — noble house structure)
- **Nemo negotiated the move himself** — his accumulated political capital as Dawnstar made the unusual demotion possible. He bargained for *obscurity* in exchange for power.
- The Trial Baron position gave him perfect cover: official empire role, no direct military reporting, enough authority to run a private mercenary intelligence network without anyone questioning his discretionary expenses

**The Vessels of Ruin operation:**
- After becoming Trial Baron, Nemo built his own private intelligence network of mercenaries — *parallel* to and *outside* the corrupted official Cormorian intelligence apparatus (which Silas Moray controls)
- Hunted the Vessels of Ruin cult for several years
- **~2 years before Osrid's return**, ambushed Harbinger Alaric and the cult at an ancient altar in a deep forgotten cave system, during their Ting-Lu incarnation ritual
- *Let the incarnation complete*, then killed Alaric in the moment of triumph
- Took **Ting-Lu** into his keeping
- Operation was a masterstroke: tactical precision, perfect timing, operational invisibility (Baradus and Goma never learn who did it; they call the unknown person "the Usurper")

**Nemo's intelligence network and the Mega-Dreamstone Shard intel `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

The same private mercenary intelligence network Nemo built to hunt the Vessels Cult has, over the years, gathered intelligence on **the scattered locations of the Mega-Dreamstone shards** (Section 9 — The Mega-Dreamstone Shard Quest). Nemo provides this intelligence to **Cadmus Umbra** through their long-standing personal trust. Umbra uses the intelligence to brief Osrid (the operational mover) after the Eden theft scene in Act I.

**The compartmentalization is tight:** Nemo provides intel to Umbra; Umbra deputizes Osrid. **Nemo does not know Osrid is the prince until the 9th Trial mutual recognition scene** (already locked v0.9.6). For most of the game, Nemo has been *supporting Osrid's clandestine objective* without knowing the operative's identity. *Yet another way Nemo is the secret savior who does not realize the full extent of what he is enabling.*

**Childhood friendship with Ambrose Caymen `[LOCKED v0.9.7]`:**

When Nemo arrived in Cormoria as a Sinnohian war-orphan (~30 years before story start) and was placed in a military-managed orphanage, **he grew up in and around the Templar Arceus order** — orphanages near Templar facilities were common as Templars handled much of the empire's civic infrastructure. **He became close friends with Ambrose Caymen**, then a young Templar acolyte and now the current Archbishop of the order. The friendship persisted into adulthood — even as Nemo rose through the military ranks to Dawnstar and then voluntarily stepped down to the 9th Trial Baron seat, even as Ambrose rose through the religious hierarchy to Archbishop. **They remained close adult friends across decades.**

**This makes Nemo's death even more emotionally consequential than v0.9.6 framed it:**

- Nemo's death scene is now also the moment **Ambrose loses one of his oldest friends.** Ambrose may not yet know of Nemo's death at the moment it happens (Baradus's operation against Nemo is highly compartmentalized), but the *eventual loss* he carries adds depth to his arc.
- **Silas Moray — who *also* served beside Nemo under Eldred for years (locked v0.9.6) — *also* knows Ambrose** (the Archbishop is one of the four most senior religious figures in the empire alongside the Viziers). Silas's lie about Nemo's career being a "punishment by the crown" (Section 7 — Ambrose Caymen) is delivered to Ambrose by *a mutual friend of both Silas and Nemo*. **Silas weaponized two friendships at once** — using his friendship with Ambrose to deliver a lie about their mutual friend Nemo. This is the cruelest specific act Silas commits, and the one that most needs his eventual redemption to earn forgiveness for.

**Congenital alexithymia — the neurological key:**

Nemo has **congenital alexithymia** — an extremely rare neurological condition that, in his specific case, makes him **unable to feel or recognize fear and intimidation.** He has full emotional range otherwise — he can love, mourn, feel curious or sorrowful or amused. **He simply cannot feel afraid.**

This is the *reason* he can hold Ting-Lu in coexistence rather than corruption. Ting-Lu, the Treasure of Earth/crushing-weight/being-buried-alive-by-inevitability, feeds on **fear**. Every previous wielder feared what Ting-Lu would do to them, and that fear was what Ting-Lu amplified to corrupt them.

**Nemo cannot feel fear. Ting-Lu has no purchase on him.**

When Nemo took Ting-Lu, the Treasure could not dominate him through its usual mechanism. Instead, for the first time in its existence, **Ting-Lu was confronted with a human it could not terrify.** And so it did something unprecedented: it *chose* him as a master, because it could be *communicated with* rather than *amplifying through*.

**Homeostatic symbiosis — the relationship:**

Nemo and Ting-Lu have lived in **homeostatic symbiosis** for the past 2 years. Ting-Lu doesn't corrupt Nemo (no fear to amplify). Nemo doesn't dominate Ting-Lu (Ting-Lu chose this freely). And the contact has been *purifying* — **Ting-Lu is developing a will of its own, beyond the negative emotions that birthed it. A Treasure is becoming a person.**

**This is the project's thesis articulated in its most extreme form.** Pokémon-as-partners-not-weapons applies *even to the Treasures of Ruin*. Under the right conditions — a Treasure that hasn't been further corrupted since its origin, paired with a human who literally cannot supply the emotion the Treasure feeds on — even pure embodied malice can become a person.

**The thesis crucial qualifier:** Ting-Lu's case is *uniquely possible*. The other three Treasures cannot be purified — Wo-Chien is too corrupted by Baradus's massacre to make it, Chi-Yu is too consumed by its incarnation conditions, Chien-Pao is the apex creation of cult ambition. **Nemo+Ting-Lu shows what is possible. It is a glimpse, not a template. And the glimpse cannot save the world.**

**The personality:**

Nemo carries himself with full emotional range minus fear. He is warm but unflappable. He grieves Eldred openly. He loves Ting-Lu sincerely. He is curious about the world and about people. He has the wisdom of a man who has been at the top of the system and walked away from it deliberately.

The world finds his absence of fear *unsettling*. People who cannot intimidate him don't know how to relate to him. Cult agents find him impervious to their normal tools. **Nemo is the calmest dangerous man anyone in Cormoria has ever met.**

**Battle ace: Manticore**
- **Unique shiny Gliscor**
- Ability: **Adaptability** (bred over generations — non-canonical for Gliscor; like the other Trial Baron aces, his ace's ability is the result of his investment of years in breeding)
- Moveset: **Beak Blast** (STAB Flying, burns on contact, brutally aggressive), **Earthquake** (STAB Ground), **Sleep Talk** + **Rest** (stall-tank loop — heal to full while still attacking)
- Adaptability-boosted Beak Blast at 100 BP effective ~200 BP equivalent. Adaptability-boosted Earthquake at level cap is devastating. Rest + Sleep Talk eliminates the three-turn vulnerability of Rest.
- Name "Manticore" — mythological hunter-beast (lion body, scorpion tail, sometimes wings). Gliscor is bat-like and predatory. The name fits both the species and Nemo's role as a hunter who waited years and struck at the perfect moment.

**The 9th Trial battle — two-phase boss:**

**Phase 1: Manticore + standard Ground-type team `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`.** The player faces Nemo's official Trial Baron lineup — a disciplined sand-engine army at the locked Trial 9 cap of 80.

| Slot | Pokémon | Ability | Item | Moves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ace** | **Manticore** — shiny Gliscor | Adaptability | Leftovers | Beak Blast / Earthquake / Rest / Sleep Talk |
| 2 | **Mega Garchomp** | Sand Force | Garchompite | Swords Dance / Earthquake / Stone Edge / Fire Fang |
| 3 | Excadrill | Sand Rush | Life Orb | Swords Dance / Earthquake / Iron Head / Rock Slide |
| 4 | Hippowdon *(lead)* | Sand Stream | Leftovers | Stealth Rock / Earthquake / Slack Off / Whirlwind |
| 5 | Swampert | Torrent | Leftovers | Earthquake / Waterfall / Ice Punch / Curse |
| 6 | Krookodile | Moxie | Choice Scarf | Earthquake / Knock Off / Stone Edge / Close Combat |

- **Strategy:** Hippowdon leads, sets the **sandstorm** (Sand Stream) and Stealth Rock. The sand powers two sweepers — Excadrill's Sand Rush doubles its Speed; Mega Garchomp's Sand Force boosts Earthquake/Stone Edge. Swampert is the bulky pivot that switches into Water and answers Grass/Dragon with Ice Punch; Krookodile (Choice Scarf + Moxie) is the speed-control revenge-killer with item-stripping Knock Off. Manticore closes — Adaptability-boosted STABs with a Rest/Sleep Talk loop that heals to full while still attacking. **Every member is Ground-typed, so the entire army is immune to its own sandstorm** — a general's disciplined force, not a gimmick.
- **The Garchomp `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`:** Nemo's Garchomp is a Sinnohian import — a Gible raised in his homeland, where the line is native — *not* a Cormorian catch. This keeps faith with Cormoria's near-extinct wild dragon population (driven out by the Tinkaton clan; Section 6) and with Glaive's failed hunt for the legendary desert Garchomp. The intended irony: Glaive, the empire's aspiring Dragon master, chases a Garchomp the whole game and ultimately never needs one — and the only Garchomp the player ever sees belongs to the Sinnohian who could simply raise one from home. Fitting, for one of the strongest trainers in the game.
- **Phase 1 victory grants the Upheaval Badge `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`** — earth thrown skyward, and the political upheaval of the Usurper; the weightiest badge name for the final standard Trial.

**Phase 2: Ting-Lu is brought out.** The moment Ting-Lu appears on the battlefield is *the moment the player realizes Nemo is the Usurper.* The mystery and the boss reveal collapse into a single moment of recognition.

**Nemo's quiet line before bringing out Ting-Lu** (suggested, exact phrasing `[OPEN]`): *"You should know who I am before you defeat me."* No gloating. A man without fear, owning what he's done.

**The mutual recognition during the Trial:**

Critically: **Nemo recognizes Osrid during the Trial battle.** Through Osrid's body language and battling style being almost identical to Eldred's. Nemo had served under Eldred for years; he saw Eldred fight, command, move. Eldred has been dead for 10 years. When Nemo faces the masked Rainhawk, he sees *Eldred's son fighting like his father.* The mask hides Osrid's face but not his father's ghost.

Nemo had already been tracking the disinformation that "Osrid is dead" — he had learned that lie was false. He just didn't know the masked Rainhawk was the prince until the Trial. **The Trial becomes a layered recognition scene — Pokemon mechanics in the foreground, two men recognizing each other secretly in the background.** Both men finish the battle anyway: the Trial is Nemo's gift to Osrid (giving the player the right to fight Ting-Lu), and Osrid's required passage through the 9th Trial.

**Nemo's death:**

After the Trial, **Baradus and Goma raid Nemo's location and kidnap Nemo and the weakened Ting-Lu.** (Baradus runs the operation himself, keeping it secret from Silas.) The player fails to stop the kidnapping.

This is the **pivotal event** that drives Osrid to:
- Commit to claiming Champion + Regent-King
- Use the empire's full military resources against the cults
- Try to rescue Nemo
- Consider that Treasures might not need to be destroyed — Nemo+Ting-Lu proved coexistence is possible

The player eventually penetrates the Sword Cult's secret headquarters and reaches Nemo. He is on death's door — they drained his blood as part of the ritual to bind Ting-Lu and prepare the conditions for Chien-Pao's resonance.

**The death scene:**
- Nemo knows Ting-Lu does not want to participate in Baradus's ritual
- He **passes Ting-Lu to Osrid** before he dies
- His final words to Ting-Lu: **"help the prince put an end to this"**
- Nemo dies, having lived 2 years in homeostatic symbiosis with a Treasure of Ruin, fully realizing what the world could be if humanity treated Pokémon as partners — and dying without seeing that world realized

**Ting-Lu's choice:**
- After the final battle, with all three other Treasures defeated, **Ting-Lu chooses to initiate the sealing ritual itself**
- This is an act of fidelity to Nemo's memory. Ting-Lu does not want to be wielded again. It does not want to risk corruption. It chooses *the dignity of being put to rest* rather than the risk of being weaponized again.
- **Ting-Lu's choice is the first conscious act of self-determination it ever made.**

**Why Nemo matters thematically:**
- He is the empire's best argument for its own meritocracy
- He is the first being to show that Treasures of Ruin can be persons, not weapons
- His death prevents the coexistence path from being achievable — Osrid sees what was possible and must seal the Treasures anyway
- His arc proves the project's thesis at its most extreme limit, and then shows the cost of being unable to extend that thesis to the rest of the world

### Reid Ashland — 2nd Trial Baron (Fire), prodigy son of House Ashland, pyrokinetic heir holding his uncle Sable's seat `[LOCKED v0.9.8 — substantial expansion of v0.9.4 entry]`

**A 23-year-old prodigy who is genuinely competent and genuinely uncertain in equal measure. Reid believes in his heart that his uncle Sable is alive and will return — and that Reid himself is simply *holding the Trial Baron seat for the man who truly earned it.* He commands his shiny Heatran "Phlegein" with reverence rather than ownership, dreams of a Fire-type sanctuary at Mt. Ceram free from the empire's combat demands, and carries the full pyrokinetic legacy of House Ashland — the first family member in a generation since Sable to be born with active fire-conjuring power. He is good-natured, philosophically opposed to violence as a problem-solving tool, neither hothead nor pushover, and visibly stretched thin by a role he was never supposed to occupy. The Trial 2 fight is one of the project's most strategically demanding early-game battles. The Mt. Ceram raid scene where Reid uses his pyrokinesis to burn Beads cultists alive in defense of his younger sisters is one of the project's most morally weighty single moments.**

**Background — Reid the prodigy:**
- 23 years old at story start, the only male Ashland heir remaining in active service
- **Three younger sisters: Rain, Brook, and River Ashland** `[LOCKED v0.9.8]` — `[OPEN]` specific ages and personalities. **None of the three sisters has pyrokinetic powers**, in keeping with the family's diminished-in-most-branches reality. The water-themed sister names against Reid's non-water name are the family's quiet open secret about who carries what gift.
- Nephew of Sable Ashland (who disappeared during Eldred's assassination — see Sable entry above)
- Has grown up under the political shadow of his family being suspected of treason — a decade of public service to defend his family's reputation
- Genuinely talented with Fire-types; his appointment as Trial Baron was a grudging empire concession that couldn't ignore his ability despite the Ashland family suspicion
- **`[v0.9.8 ADDITION]` Reid is the first Ashland in a generation since his uncle Sable to be born with *active* pyrokinetic powers** — the family's foundational supernatural gift, the literal ability to conjure and direct fire. Per Section 12 — House Ashland: pyrokinesis has diminished across most modern Ashland branches; **the determining factor each generation of who leads the family is who has the strongest pyrokinetic legacy and the deepest bond-potential with Fire-type Pokemon.** Sable's pyrokinesis was the strongest of his generation; Reid's is the strongest of his. **This is why leadership fell to Reid immediately after Sable's disappearance** — not just by birth order, but by the family's strict succession rules. *Reid was marked from birth.* The three sisters Rain, Brook, and River, lacking pyrokinesis, were never candidates by family rule.

**Personality and voice `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **Confident with visible cracks.** Reid's public competence is real but he does not fully trust it. The strain shows in unguarded moments — a small pause before a decision, a brief glance at the empty chair where Sable should be. He is *aware* his confidence is fragile, and he chooses to act anyway. That choice is itself a kind of courage.
- **No illusions about Ashland's standing or his own current capabilities.** He knows the family is under suspicion. He knows his own combat ceiling is lower than what the Trial Baron seat demands of a full master. He does not pretend otherwise. **This honesty with himself is one of his most likable traits** — *he is not posturing*, and the player feels it.
- **Good-natured at baseline.** Kind, not bitter, not cynical despite the years of slander. The treason suspicion against his family did not curdle him; it sharpened his determination to *demonstrate* the family's actual character through his own conduct. Players who interact with Reid casually find him warm, patient, and quietly funny.
- **Feels stretched thin; "not where I truly belong."** The Trial Baron role is a *holding pattern* in Reid's own mind, not his destination. He carries it dutifully but without identification — he is *playing a role*, and the role does not fit who he believes he is meant to become.
- **Believes Sable is alive and will return.** *This is the private hope that keeps him going.* He has no proof. The decade of silence would have broken most relatives' faith. **Reid's hasn't broken.** He believes — quietly, without performance — that his uncle survived whatever happened during Eldred's assassination, and that one day Sable will come home. *Until then, Reid is the placeholder.* The bible's locked Sable-return arc vindicates this belief; Reid is *correct*, though he doesn't know how correct until Sable actually returns ~70% through the story.
- **Dreams beyond combat.** Reid's personal aspiration is to discover more Fire-type Pokemon and **cultivate Mt. Ceram into a place where Fire-types can live in harmony and peace.** He believes "Pokemon have destinies beyond battle" and wishes to create environments where they can thrive **without constantly serving as combat surrogates for the petty feuds of human beings or being used for large-scale wars that only benefit humans.** This worldview is *foundational*, not casual — it shapes how he raises his team, how he speaks to Phlegein, and how he intends to live after retirement.
- **Neither pacifist nor hothead nor pushover.** *Measured, deliberate, doesn't lead with fighting to solve problems.* But he does not avoid combat when the situation requires it — he simply prefers any other route first. **When fighting is the right answer, he fights, and he fights well.** When it isn't, he doesn't.
- **Reveres Phlegein but does not idolize him.** He knows his shiny Heatran is exceptional — Mythical-tier potential, "power that is potentially unlimited" — and treats Phlegein with the careful regard of a young master who has not yet earned what he carries. *He does not flaunt the ace.* When Phlegein deploys, it is with a brief bow of the head and a quiet *"Are you ready, friend?"* — the formal register a prodigy reserves for the partner that has made his rise possible.

**House Ashland's pyrokinetic legacy and Reid's place in it `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

House Ashland's foundational identity is that they are **a pyrokinetic family** — humans who can physically conjure and direct fire, not merely train Fire-type Pokemon. Originating in Naljo, the family fled the legendary Varaneous's coercive demand that they weaponize their power against other humans (Section 12 — House Ashland Naljo backstory, expanded v0.9.8). **The family's founding moral act was refusing to burn people alive at a tyrant's direction.** Reid's worldview — Pokemon have destinies beyond battle, fire should not be made to serve petty human violence — is the **same moral refusal his ancestors made, applied to a new domain**. Reid is not a deviation from family tradition; he is its truest inheritor.

**The pyrokinesis itself, in Reid:**
- Reid can physically conjure and direct fire. This is *real*, not metaphorical. **Not a routine combat capability** — he does not deploy pyrokinesis in standard Trial battles or political appearances; his Pokemon partnership is the *appropriate* combat vector and the family's modern public-facing identity.
- The power *is* there, present and accessible. He simply chooses, in the conventional course of life, not to use it.
- Most modern Cormorians know nothing of House Ashland's Naljo history. They treat the Ashlands as another long-standing noble house. **The pyrokinetic legacy is therefore invisible to the general public** — known only to the family itself, to other deeply-informed senior figures (Cadmus Umbra; possibly Kimaris Langerin via his exorcist consultancy work; possibly Mordred Nightfall from old family-to-family acquaintance), and eventually to the player when the bible's lore surfaces in the story.

**The Mt. Ceram raid pyrokinesis scene `[LOCKED v0.9.8 — narrative; engineering OPEN]`:**

**The player witnesses Reid use his pyrokinesis exactly once in the game**, during the Mt. Ceram raid arc (Section 8 — Beads Cult attack on the Ashland Labyrinth's lava-pool Leyline point; Section 10 — Mt. Ceram raid placement). The scene structure:

- The Beads Cult is raiding the Ashland Labyrinth as part of their attempt to reach Chi-Yu's Leyline incarnation point at the deep lava pool
- A group of cultists, breaking off from the main raid, has cornered **Rain, Brook, and River** (Reid's three younger sisters) and is attempting to harm them — either as leverage, as tactical hostages, or as opportunistic violence against the family
- **The player and Reid arrive together — *just as Reid uses his power.*** The player arrives *during* the act, not after. Pokemon battles with other cultists during the broader raid had delayed the player and Reid by minutes that mattered. **Conventional combat had not been fast enough.**
- **Reid burns the cultists alive with directed fire** — saving his sisters, in front of the player.
- **The aftermath is quiet.** Reid does not celebrate. He does not speak much. *He had hoped never to use this power that way.* The player gathers what happened and what it cost him. **Show-Don't-Tell: the act *and* the cost both shown plainly.**
- **The player's emotional center of the scene is *moral helplessness*.** The player feels — quietly, without dialog explicitly stating it — that *if they had arrived slightly earlier*, Pokemon battles alone could have saved the sisters, and Reid would not have had to make this choice. **This is the first moment in the game where the player's "Pokemon-battles-as-the-better-way" framework fails in real time** — not because the framework is wrong, but because real violence sometimes outruns it. **The scene quietly teaches that the partnership thesis is a *moral aspiration the world resists*, not a guarantee.** That landing deepens every subsequent partnership beat by reminding the player that the right answer doesn't always work fast enough.

**Structural significance:** This is one of the project's most morally weighty single moments and **one of the very few on-screen instances of a sympathetic main character killing humans directly.** The act is morally legible (defense of children against immediate violent attack on them), but the project will have meaningfully crossed a tonal threshold once this scene ships — *real-stakes violence with consequences*, not stylized Pokemon-mediated combat. It works *because* it is shown with cost, restraint, and aftermath, not in triumph. **The Ashlands fled Naljo because they refused to burn people alive at a tyrant's direction. Reid uses his power on his own moral terms to defend the most vulnerable members of his family. The moral logic completes across generations** — the ancestors who refused Varaneous would *recognize and approve* of Reid's choice.

`[OPEN]` Specific dialogue for the aftermath beat — recommendation: minimal. Reid says little; the player learns to read his silence.
`[OPEN]` Specific cultist team(s) the player fights immediately before the scene (the encounters that delay them)
`[OPEN]` Whether the sisters' relationship to Reid is further developed in scenes before this moment, or whether they are present primarily *here* — recommendation: brief earlier scene(s) at the Ashland Labyrinth so the sisters are not strangers to the player when the danger lands

**The historical irony of the treason suspicion `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

The Cormorian common-knowledge view that "House Ashland probably helped assassinate Eldred Nightfall" is **not just unfair — it is *inverted from the family's actual character*.** Most Cormorians don't know House Ashland's Naljo history. They treat the Ashlands as just another long-standing noble house, and when post-Eldred suspicion crystallized, they repeated the slander *without any reference to the family's foundational identity.* **The people slandering the Ashlands could not even articulate what they are getting wrong, because they do not know the history.** The Ashlands fled their homeland *specifically to avoid being made instruments of violence against innocents*; the empire now suspects them of having abetted exactly such violence. **The historical ignorance is itself part of the tragedy** — the Ashlands are slandered by people who would *change their minds* if they understood what the family actually is. *That is sadder than simple injustice.* Reid carries this weight quietly; the player learns to feel it as the lore surfaces.

**The Trial battle (Trial 2) — full team locked v0.9.8:**

- **Level cap:** 25 (per the locked Trial cap structure)
- **Format:** standard 6v6 single-trainer battle
- **Design intent:** *break the obvious counter.* Water-pickers find their Water-type one-shot by Heatran's Freeze-Dry through Passho. The supporting team reinforces this trap with multiple layers of weather, hazards, intimidation, and burn pressure. **The fight forces team-building beyond starter monotony.** Per the existing v0.9.4 lock: Frigibax pickers worst off (Ice resists Ice; Dragon resists Steel); Teddiursa pickers have Fighting-coverage path through Ursaring; Tinkatink pickers have bulk but no super-effective punch.
- **Engine cost is minimal** — only one custom species ability override (Heatran Earth Eater); every other team member uses canonical abilities. Per-trainer move grants where needed.

| **Ace** | **Phlegein** — shiny Heatran | genderless | **Earth Eater** (custom override; canonical Flash Fire is replaced by Ground-immunity) | Torch Song / Magnet Bomb / Freeze-Dry / **Scorching Sands** | **Passho Berry** | Named *Phlegein* (Greek φλέγειν, "to blaze / to burn") — locked v0.9.8. Mostly-special attacker; massive SpA. Scorching Sands is the **trap-closer**: Ground-type special coverage on a Ground-immune ace. Rock-types who wall Fire get hit by Ground. The 30% burn chance compounds the team's burn pressure. Torch Song raises SpA per use → escalating threat. Freeze-Dry through Passho Berry one-shots Water counters. The 4-move kit has no obvious safe answer. |

Eviolite makes her surprisingly tanky for a mid-stage. Extreme Speed +2 priority Normal STAB punishes setup-into-cleanup play. Intimidate stacks via switch-pivoting to keep player physical attackers debuffed. Snarl debuffs player SpA. *Across the fight, Reid can debuff both attack stats* (Intimidate physical + Snarl special). Morning Sun → 66% recovery in sun. Lore-perfect ancient guardian dog for an "ancient divine family of Fire magic users." |

Drought on entry → 5 turns of sun (boosts team Fire damage, halves player Water damage). Lava Plume burn pressure. Yawn forces sleep-or-switch. Body Press leverages massive Defense. Earth Power coverage. *The slow, ancient, magma-shelled tortoise that has lived inside Mt. Ceram so long that nothing surprises him* — the Ashland Labyrinth resident with no equal. |

**Team-level strategic architecture:**

- **Sun architecture:** Torkoal Drought (primary, 5 turns on entry) + Magmar Sunny Day (backup if sun lapses or Torkoal removed). **The team operates in sun more often than not** — boosts team Fire damage, halves player Water damage. The Trial 2 trap is precisely that *the obvious Water counter doesn't work because Reid built specifically against it.*
- **Hazard layer:** Coalossal Stealth Rock chips every player switch-in by 12.5-50%. Compounds Reid's stall pressure.
- **Burn pressure:** Phlegein Scorching Sands (30% burn special) + Magmar Flame Body (burn on contact, passive) + Torkoal Lava Plume (30% burn). **Three independent burn vectors** — player physical attackers get debuffed across the fight.
- **Stat debuff layer:** Arcanine Intimidate (player Atk on Arcanine entry, stacks via switches) + Snarl (player SpA on attack). *Both attack stats can be reduced.*
- **Pivot mechanics:** Arcanine switches in/out to re-apply Intimidate; Coalossal Rapid Spin clears player hazards; Torkoal Yawn forces switches into Stealth Rock.
- **Closing threat layer:** Coalossal Weakness Policy boom turn + Phlegein Torch Song escalation + Arcanine Extreme Speed priority cleanup. **Three distinct win conditions, each requiring different player counter-strategies to neutralize.**

**The strategic teaching:** *no single coverage axis carries the player through.* Per the locked design intent, the fight "forces team-building beyond starter monotony." The player must bring multiple coverage angles, manage weather, and out-think Reid's traps. **It is the fight that makes the player a real trainer, not just a starter-runner.**

**The character resonance:** disciplined, layered, defensive-first, *built to prove competence under pressure*. The team is built the way Reid lives — carefully, deliberately, with multiple fallbacks. A decade of defending his family's reputation produced *exactly this kind of trainer*. **And yet Reid does not love the team because it wins; he loves the team because they are his.** *His personal dream is to retire with all of them to Mt. Ceram and live out his sanctuary vision together.*

**Reid's combat voice (pre- and post-battle):**
- **Pre-battle (controlled, formal-friendly):** Reid greets the player with quiet warmth. He acknowledges the player's progress through Trial 1, briefly references the difficulty of Cormoria's Trials, and deploys Phlegein with a small ceremonial gesture. *Are you ready, friend?* — the locked register for Phlegein deployment.
- **During battle (focused, minimal):** Reid speaks rarely during the fight itself; the team's strategic depth speaks for him.
- **Post-defeat (confidence cracks slightly; warmth surfaces):** Reid concedes openly, with no excuses or wounded pride. *That was masterfully done.* He grants the **Smelt Badge**. **If the player has shown particular ingenuity or kindness toward their Pokemon during the fight, Reid notes it briefly — recognizing something of his own worldview in the player.** The conversation is short; Reid does not linger over defeat. *He has work to return to.*

**Mid-game retirement (~70% through the story) `[LOCKED, expanded v0.9.8]`:**

- After Sable's return (Section 7 — Sable Ashland), Reid retires from his Trial Baron seat
- Returns to study under **Cadmus Umbra** as a full-time student
- **Keeps his entire Trial 2 team** — he does not hand any Pokemon off to Sable or anyone else. *He loves them all too much to ever let any of them go.* The team accompanies him into his scholar arc.
- His personal dream: discover more Fire-type Pokemon, cultivate Mt. Ceram into a place where Fire-types can live in harmony and peace
- **The overworld interaction tone shifts visibly after retirement** — Reid becomes *more relaxed* with Phlegein in scholar-mode than he was in Trial-Baron-public-figure mode. **The shift is itself character:** Reid's career arc is "prodigy son shouldering disgrace → free scholar"; his overworld-interaction tone with Phlegein tracks the same arc. *His real life begins here.*
- This is a **complete character arc** — Trial Baron → student → scholar → eventual Fire-type sanctuary cultivator — that the player witnesses for a Trial Baron, an unusual narrative move that elevates the Trial House structure overall and **vindicates Reid's lifelong belief that he was holding the seat for Sable.** Once Sable returns, Reid is *free.*

### Kimaris Langerin — 1st Trial Baron (Ghost), Reserve Champion of Cormoria, patriarch of House Langerin, spiritualist-sorcerer-exorcist `[LOCKED v0.9.8 — substantial rewrite of v0.9.4 "former Champion" framing]`

**One of the project's most thematically central characters — and the reason the player faces him first. Kimaris is not a former Champion; he is Cormoria's designated *Reserve Champion*, the man who would assume the Champion seat if Rhydia were killed. He earned this designation by defeating all four Viziers in succession and then tying with Champion Mordred Nightfall in their direct match — and then voluntarily renouncing the Champion seat in favor of the Trial Baron seat and the Langerin patriarchy. He is a spiritualist, a sorcerer, and an exorcist — a Templar Arceus consultant for hauntings the lesser priests cannot handle. He is over-the-top affectionate with his Pokemon in a way that quietly states the project's entire partnership thesis without saying it. He is Cadmus Umbra's lifelong dearest friend. He is one of the highest-value cult targets in Cormoria precisely because his institutional roles span House, Trial, Necropolis, and Templar consultancy — and he is therefore kept deliberately separate from the Resistance Triad's operational core by Cadmus, as risk mitigation. Most of this is invisible to the player at Trial 1. What is visible is a goofy, loving Master trainer hugging his shiny rock Pokemon and calling him "the bestest most powerful most wonderful legion of ferocious spooksters." That display, this early in the game, is the partnership thesis taught by example.**

**The Reserve Champion designation `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **Kimaris is NOT a former Champion.** This is a correction of the v0.9.4 framing. He has never held the Champion seat. He is Cormoria's designated **Reserve Champion** — the line of succession if Rhydia were killed or rendered incapable.
- **How he earned the designation (8 years before game start):** Kimaris fought through all four Viziers of Cormoria in succession and *defeated each of them* in formal challenge matches. He then fought the reigning Champion **Mordred Nightfall** directly — and **the match ended in a tie.** (Mordred had held the Champion seat for ~45 years at that point, and was at his still-formidable late peak. A tie against him was an extraordinary accomplishment.)
- **The voluntary renunciation:** Immediately after the Mordred tie, Kimaris **informed the Concordance publicly that he had no desire to pursue the Champion seat.** He asked instead to be granted (a) recognition as a Trial Baron, and (b) the Langerin family patriarchy over his older siblings (Kimaris was born as the third son and would not normally have inherited the patriarchy).
- **The decree — Rhydia's first major act as Regent-Empress, at age 12 `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:** The Concordance honored Kimaris's request — and the formal decree was issued by **Princess Regent Rhydia Cormoria, then 12 years old.** This was her **first significant act as the empire's acting authority** following Eldred's assassination two years prior and Pierra's withdrawal to the Villa. *A twelve-year-old girl was now the acting queen of the entire empire, and her first major public decree was to recognize a Reserve Champion's voluntary renunciation, his Trial Baron seat, and his elevation over his older brothers to the Langerin patriarchy.* This event is structurally significant in Rhydia's character backstory — Section 6 — Rhydia (cross-referenced; the early-authority arc is now properly anchored to this specific decree).
- **Timeline:** 8 years pre-game (Kimaris tie + renunciation + Rhydia's age-12 decree) → 5 years pre-game (Rhydia at 15 defeats Mordred and becomes Champion in her own right) → 2 years pre-game (Rhydia defeats Kimaris's Marshadow at level 100 in a public unrestricted match, cementing her legitimacy). The 3-year gap between the Mordred tie and Rhydia's own Champion seat was a period during which Mordred remained Champion of record and Kimaris held the Reserve designation by formal decree.
- **Why he renounced the Champion seat:** Kimaris's spiritual worldview (see personality below) emphasizes service over status. The Trial Baron seat and Langerin patriarchy let him serve in the ways most natural to his gift — guarding the Mirroh Necropolis, conducting exorcisms and supernatural consultancy, presiding over Ghost-type training as a Master. **He could be Champion; he chose to be himself.**

**The two older Langerin brothers `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **Dale Langerin** and **Gram Langerin** — Kimaris's two older brothers, the *first* and *second* sons of the previous Langerin patriarch. Both are *lesser trainers* the player fights as opening encounters in the Mirroh Necropolis before reaching Kimaris at the Trial 1 chamber. They are minor characters — no further backstory required. Their place in the Langerin succession was supplanted by Rhydia's age-12 decree elevating Kimaris over them; whatever their reaction to that decree was, **they have accepted it.** ([OPEN] minor flavor for their dialog and team composition; cap 18 like Kimaris.)

**Background — House and lineage:**
- **Head of House Langerin** (patriarch by Rhydia's decree) — Ghost-type masters, one of the **five-oldest noble houses** of Cormoria (Section 12). Keepers of the **Mirroh Necropolis** (which decays into "Mirroh Base Camp Graveyard" in DM's era).
- **Family naming convention: occult-traditional names** (Kimaris is a Goetia demon — one of the 72 demons of the Ars Goetia; the older brothers Dale and Gram follow the same pattern).
- The Necropolis contains a **sealed gate to the Distortion World** (Giratina's realm). House Langerin are the keepers of this gate — ghosts are creatures between worlds, the gate is between worlds, the family literally guards a wall between realms.

**The implication for the project's tone:** Kimaris has the power to *conjure and commune with the dead and lost souls*. This is genuinely supernatural — more than typing affinity, this is *real magic* in a world that mostly doesn't use it. The project is comfortable with this tone (Pokemon canonically has psychics, oracles, ghost-trainers); Kimaris just pushes the supernatural register slightly more explicit than usual.

**Personality and worldview `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **A spiritualist who believes in the *bigger picture* and that people should not fear death.** Kimaris's spiritual practice centers on the continuity between living and dead — he feels love, joy, and sorrow for both equally. This is *not* morbid; it is *generous*. He grieves the dead because he loved them; he loves the living because they too will one day be among the dead. **Death is not a tragedy in Kimaris's worldview — it is a transition, and the work of a Langerin is to honor and ease that transition.**
- **Tremendous empathy.** He is a *keen observer of human nature* with a deep capacity for feeling what others feel. This sensitivity is what makes him both an exceptional medium (he reads the emotional residue of the dead as easily as he reads the living) and an exceptional teacher (he meets the player exactly where they are, without judgment, without pressing).
- **Deep, almost fanatical reverence for Cadmus Umbra.** Kimaris considers Cadmus his **intellectual idol and dearest friend.** The two grew up together at the academy — they are roughly the same age and spent most of their youth in academic environments together. They collaborate across many subjects; Kimaris's trust in Cadmus's ideals is **resolute.** *Kimaris would do anything Cadmus asked.* (This relationship is significant for the Resistance-Triad-adjacency lock below — see also Section 7 — Cadmus Umbra, cross-referenced.)
- **Aware of the player's importance but does not press.** Kimaris perceives that the masked Rainhawk Alban is *unusual* — possibly more than he claims — but he does not press the player for identity or backstory. His trust in Cadmus (who he knows has taken an interest in this trainer) is sufficient.
- **Aware of the Treasures of Ruin and the cults' machinations.** Kimaris is not naive. He understands the supernatural landscape of the empire including the active threats. He has been *actively defending* House Langerin's secrets and the Necropolis against Sword and Bead Cult infiltration attempts for years, and has so far successfully prevented either cult from gaining real intel on the family's mysteries or penetrating the Necropolis grounds.
- **A goofy, over-the-top affectionate side with his Pokemon.** Kimaris talks to Crowley *the way some people talk to cats, dogs, or newborn children* — in a constant flow of affectionate baby-voice praise, polishing his rock, hugging him, calling him things like *"the bestest most powerful most wonderful legion of ferocious spooksters to ever exist since the creation of the universe!"* He sees Crowley as a *newborn* (which Crowley is — a freshly-conjured Spiritomb is the youngest possible incarnation of a 108-soul-aggregate entity, ironically) and showers him with the love and affection a parent gives a baby. *This is not performative; it is genuinely how Kimaris feels.*
- **A deep stoic side surfaces in serious moments.** When the supernatural threat is real, when an exorcism is in progress, when the Necropolis is under threat, the goofy register *vanishes* and a quiet, ancient-feeling gravity takes its place. The same man who hugs his rock Pokemon is also the man who can stand at the Distortion gate alone and hold it shut by sheer spiritual presence. *Both registers are real.*

**Vocation — spiritualist, sorcerer, exorcist, Templar consultant `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **Spiritualist:** Kimaris's primary public-facing identity. He communes with the dead, performs séances and rituals, and is the empire's most trusted authority on matters of the soul's passage.
- **Sorcerer:** Kimaris's *summoning* practice — the conjuring work that produced Crowley after thousands of failed attempts (see below) is genuine sorcery. He is one of very few Cormorians who can pull souls and entities across the threshold into the material realm.
- **Exorcist:** When a place or person is haunted by something that does not belong — or by something that *does* belong but should not be active — Kimaris and the Langerin family's top mediums are called in.
- **Templar Arceus consultancy `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:** **Archbishop Ambrose Caymen** (Section 7 — Ambrose Caymen) regularly calls on Kimaris and the Langerin mediums to deal with hauntings and strange supernatural phenomena that the lesser Templar priests cannot handle. This is an *ongoing institutional relationship*, not ad-hoc. It creates a three-way infrastructure web among the empire's senior institutions: **House Raptora** engineered the Braviary mount system (Section 12 — Raptora services), **the Templar Arceus order** operationalizes that system + maintains the empire's daily religious-civic infrastructure (Section 4 — Templar Order), and **House Langerin** handles the supernatural-affairs consultancy for problems beyond the lesser priests' capability. *Three old institutions, three complementary specialties, one woven empire.* Note: this also means **Kimaris and Ambrose have a working relationship that long predates the late-game Necropolis Assault** where they fight side-by-side against the Sword Cult — the Assault alliance is the late-game escalation of an institutional friendship already in place for years.

**Relationship to the Resistance Triad — adjacent, deliberately kept separate `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

The empire's covert Resistance Triad consists of **Cadmus Umbra (strategist), Nemo Korolev (operator), and Falco Raptora (institutional-reach senior counsel)** (Section 7 — Cadmus, Nemo, Falco). They operate against both Ruin Cults outside the official Concordance framework.

**Kimaris is *adjacent* to the Triad — not in it.** This separation is *deliberate tradecraft* on Cadmus's part. The reasoning:

- **Kimaris's institutional exposure is enormous.** He is publicly the Trial 1 Baron, the Langerin patriarch, the Reserve Champion, the Templar Arceus's go-to exorcist, the keeper of the Mirroh Necropolis. He is *visible*. He has *targets painted on him* by every cult faction.
- **The cults already factor him into their long-term strategy.** The Sword Cult knows he holds Marshadow; the Bead Cult knows he has Templar Arceus consultancy access. **He is one of the highest-value compromise targets in Cormoria.**
- **Therefore Cadmus deliberately compartmentalizes him out of operational specifics.** Kimaris shares intel with Cadmus about cult infiltration attempts against House Langerin and the Necropolis (which is genuinely useful information for the Triad), and Kimaris is *aware* the cults are an active threat, but **he is not told the Triad's operational plans, Nemo's deeper activities, or the specifics of Triad coordination.** This is **risk mitigation** — if Kimaris were captured, drugged, broken, or otherwise compromised, the Triad's existence would survive intact.
- **Kimaris does not know he is being compartmentalized.** Cadmus's loving deception is precisely the kind of asymmetry the lifelong-friendship-and-spy-craft tension produces. The two men's bond is *unreservedly* warm and resolute on Kimaris's side; Cadmus protects that bond by holding back exactly the things that would put Kimaris in greater danger.
- **This same compartmentalization pattern exists with Bridget Nightfall** (Section 7 — Bridget) — also Cadmus's individual contact, also anti-cult-aware, also kept structurally outside the Triad. *Cadmus has individual contacts beyond the Triad's core, and he keeps each compartment separate from the others by design.*

**Why Kimaris is the player's first Trial Baron — partnership-thesis modeling `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

The Trial 1 placement is *deliberate.* Kimaris was chosen as the first Trial Baron the player encounters specifically because **he most clearly models what a true bond between a Master trainer and their Pokemon looks like.** Before the player reaches Mt. Ceram, before the Hermit ritual, before the Crabominable adoption, before any of the partnership-thesis beats that the rest of the game develops — *the player sees Kimaris hug his rock Pokemon and call him the bestest most powerful most wonderful legion of ferocious spooksters in the universe.* That display *is the thesis statement of the game compressed into one character's overworld behavior.* The player sees what a partnership looks like, modeled by a Master, before they have any other framework for evaluating it. **The first Trial Baron is the project's earliest Show-Don't-Tell partnership-thesis demonstration.**

**The Trial battle (Trial 1) — design intent `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **Level cap: 18.** This is the first Trial — the early-game.
- **Format:** standard 6v6 single-trainer battle.
- **The team is *deliberately calibrated as a teaching fight*** — NOT Kimaris's actual best play. Kimaris's true team (the higher-level, Marshadow-led roster) is locked as a *post-Champion final-act side quest*, not the Trial 1 fight. The Trial 1 team is what Kimaris has specifically set up *to test the player.*
- **The Curse strategy is the design centerpiece.** Five of the six team members carry Curse. **Kimaris uses his other five Pokemon essentially as pawns** to whittle the player down with stacked Curse residual damage and Will-O-Wisp burns, then **saves Crowley for last** as the final stall-and-finisher.
- **Design goal:** challenge the player reasonably but allow victory with a *decent variety* of teams. **No button-mashing path.** The player must *think* about Curse residual, prioritize threats (especially Shedinja), and read priority/pivot patterns. **Fire-type and/or Fairy-type coverage helps.** Pure-Ghost teams suffer. Players who came prepared with type-coverage discipline succeed; players who didn't get sent back to think.

**The Trial 1 team `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

| Slot | Pokémon | Gender | Ability | Moveset | Item | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ace** | **shiny Spiritomb, "Crowley"** | ♂ (treated as male in narrative voice; canonically genderless species — Kimaris uses he/him) | **Prankster** (custom override; canonical: Pressure/Infiltrator hidden) | Curse / Strength Sap / Shadow Claw / Protect | `[OPEN]` | The locked ace. Prankster + Curse priority → guaranteed Curse residual on player. Strength Sap heals and debuffs. Protect stalls Curse ticks. The genuine difficulty piece — saved for last. *Kimaris's newest conjured partner, treated by him as a newborn baby.* |
| 2 | Dusclops | ♀ | Pressure | Shadow Sneak / Will-O-Wisp / Curse / Recover | **Eviolite** | Defensive stall pivot. Eviolite + Will-O-Wisp burn + Curse residual + Recover sustain = the team's secondary stall threat alongside Crowley. Pressure burns the player's PP on every targeted move — a quiet additional stall vector. |
| 3 | Shedinja | ♂ | Wonder Guard | Astonish / Infestation / Will-O-Wisp / Curse | **King's Rock** | **The type-coverage gate.** Wonder Guard makes Shedinja immune to anything not super-effective — Fire, Flying, Rock, Ghost, or Dark required to KO. Astonish (Ghost priority, 30% flinch) + King's Rock (10% flinch per hit) = priority flinch-cheese. Infestation traps the player in. **Curse on Shedinja is intentional self-immolation** — Shedinja's 1 HP suicides on Curse use, but Curse-lock is applied to the player's active Pokemon. *Strategic late-Shedinja sacrifice.* |
| 4 | Honedge | ♂ | No Guard | Shadow Sneak / Metal Claw / Aerial Ace / Reflect | **Muscle Band** | Anti-Fairy and team-support pivot. Metal Claw hits Fairy-type counters; Reflect halves physical damage team-wide. No Guard guarantees all hits (both ways). Muscle Band boosts physical damage 10%. *Item-diversity choice* — could have been Eviolite (Kimaris already has two of those). |
| 5 | Gastly | ♀ | Levitate | Night Shade / Confuse Ray / Curse / Parting Shot | **Eviolite** | Stall pivot — Eviolite on first-stage Gastly is *substantially* bulkier than the player will expect. Night Shade does fixed level-18 damage (steady chip). Confuse Ray + Curse residual + Parting Shot pivot. Gastly weakens the active player Pokemon then switches in a counter via Parting Shot. |
| 6 | Dhelmise | genderless | **Steelworker** (canonical hidden) | Astonish / Smart Strike / Razor Leaf / Curse | **Quick Claw** | **Coverage breaker.** Smart Strike (never-miss Steel) hits Fairy counters. Razor Leaf provides Grass coverage for Ground/Rock/Water players. Steelworker +50% boosts Smart Strike specifically. Quick Claw lets Dhelmise occasionally outspeed despite being slow. Curse usable in late game when Dhelmise is low (substantial HP can survive 1-2 self-Curse uses for residual chip-out). |

**Team-level strategy and difficulty design:**

- **Curse residual stacking** — five team members carry Curse. Even though a single Curse doesn't stack on the same target, **Kimaris cycles his Pokemon so each one applies *fresh* Curse to whichever player Pokemon is active.** Across a long fight, the player's entire team gets Curse-chipped to a quarter HP per turn at minimum.
- **Will-O-Wisp burns** (Dusclops + Shedinja) — the player's physical attackers lose half attack damage to burn. *Counters non-Fire physical attackers specifically* — Fire-type physical attackers are immune to burn and remain a key counter.
- **Shadow Sneak finishing** (Dusclops, Honedge, Crowley) — consistent Ghost priority for picking off Curse-weakened threats.
- **Anti-Fairy coverage** (Honedge Metal Claw, Dhelmise Smart Strike) — players who bring Fairy types to wreck the Ghost/Dark synergy get punished by Steel coverage.
- **Anti-Wonder-Guard gate** (Shedinja) — players must have type-effective coverage for Shedinja or be hard-walled by it. *The fight literally tests whether the player has built a coverage-disciplined team.*
- **Reflect support** (Honedge) — halved incoming physical damage team-wide, multiplying the effective HP of Kimaris's stall game.
- **Pivot mechanics** (Gastly Parting Shot, Dhelmise Quick Claw) — Kimaris has multiple ways to bring in counters at advantage.
- **The whole architecture is *stall, status, and threat-priority*** — the player wins by recognizing the Curse-residual pattern, prioritizing Shedinja with the right coverage, and bringing Fire or Fairy or both. *This is a thinking fight at the lowest cap in the game.*

**Crowley — the newest conjured partner `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

- **Crowley is a unique shiny Spiritomb** brought into the material realm "after thousands of failed summoning attempts" — Crowley exists only because the Langerin family worked at his summoning for generations. **Kimaris's view of Crowley: he is the *shining fruition of numerous conjuring experiments* across the family's history.** A *newborn* (which Crowley canonically is — a freshly-conjured Spiritomb is the youngest possible incarnation of a 108-soul-aggregate entity, ironically) treated with all the love and affection a parent gives a baby.
- **Names "Crowley" — Aleister Crowley, the occultist.** Following the Langerin family naming convention.
- **Prankster is custom.** Canonical Spiritomb abilities are Pressure (regular) and Infiltrator (hidden). The Prankster override is a per-trainer-Pokemon ability override (Section 11 — Player-Driven Design Over Mainline Canonicity). Engineering task #71 (added in v0.9.8; see Section 14).
- **Crowley is genderless canonically but is *treated as male* in narrative voice** — Kimaris uses he/him pronouns for him and refers to him as a son.
- **Crowley is NOT Kimaris's true ace.** Marshadow is the Langerin family's generational ace and the apex of Kimaris's true combat strength (see Marshadow section below). Crowley is Kimaris's *newest* partner — the freshest conjuring success, the most loved-on baby. **The Trial 1 fight uses Crowley as the calibrated-for-the-player ace; the post-game side quest fight uses Marshadow as the true ace.**

**Overworld interactions with Crowley `[LOCKED v0.9.8 — Section 11 ace-bonding lock]`:**

Kimaris's overworld interaction register with Crowley is **over-the-top goofy-affectionate baby-voice praise**, with a *deep stoic* contrast surfacing only in serious moments. Per Section 11 — Ace-Bonding Overworld Interactions, this is one of the project's most distinctive bond-registers. The voice quality: the way some people talk to cats, dogs, or newborn children — *constant flow* of affectionate praise, polishing the rock, hugging him, superlative-stacked exclamations. Example tone (not literal locked dialog): *"You are the bestest most powerful most wonderful legion of ferocious spooksters to ever exist since the creation of the universe!"* The player observes this **before** meeting any other Trial Baron and **before** most of the game's partnership-thesis content develops — establishing the thesis by *example*, not exposition. When serious supernatural threats are active (an exorcism, a Necropolis breach, the late-game Sword Cult assault), the goofy register *vanishes* and Kimaris's stoic gravity surfaces. *Both registers are real.*

**The Marshadow generational ace `[LOCKED]`:**

House Langerin holds **Marshadow** (Ghost/Fighting Mythical) as the family's generational ace — passed down within the Langerin lineage as the most powerful asset of their Ghost-tradition (Section 2 — Generational Aces of the Senior Noble Houses).

- **Marshadow's lore-resonance with House Langerin is precise:** Marshadow canonically slips through underworlds and merges with the shadows of others. House Langerin keeps the Mirroh Necropolis and the sealed gate to the Distortion World. *The Pokemon and the family share the same spiritual register.*
- **Marshadow does not appear in the standard Trial 1 battle** — Crowley the Spiritomb is the Trial ace at level cap 18. Marshadow is held in reserve and deployed only in extreme circumstances.
- **Two years before the game's story starts, Kimaris brought out Marshadow against Rhydia in a public, unrestricted-level Champion's-defense match.** This was *not* a Trial battle — it was an exhibition or political-stakes match between the reigning Champion (Rhydia) and the Reserve Champion (Kimaris) where the level cap did not apply. Kimaris's Marshadow was at level 100; he brought his full Reserve-Champion roster. **Rhydia won.** This victory cemented her Championship legitimacy and triggered her two-year surge in popularity (Section 7 — Rhydia). Note: the Reserve-Champion-vs-reigning-Champion match was Kimaris testing whether Rhydia was *truly* ready to hold the seat — *his Marshadow deployment was the highest-stakes test he could give her*, and her victory proved she could carry the position even against the empire's deepest available challenge.
- **The cults learned that House Langerin has a Mythical-tier ace through this match** and have factored this into their long-term strategy ever since. The Sword Cult has avoided direct confrontation with the Langerin family despite their religious-political opposition partly because Marshadow's existence makes such confrontation expensive.

**Kimaris's true heritage — the hidden progenitor lineage `[LOCKED v0.9.4]`:**

Kimaris does not know this in the present-day story, but it is canonical to the project's cosmology:

- **Kimaris is a direct descendant of *both* Lethys (the Blue Moon Hermit) AND Madame Roma / Roma Langerin** (Section 7 — Blue Moon Hermit; Section 7 — Madame Roma). His Langerin bloodline traces back to the pact-era when Lethys and Roma had children together, founding House Langerin.
- **He is therefore a distant Celestica descendant** through the Lethys line — and a *doubly-blessed Langerin descendant* through the Roma line. **His bloodline literally converges Cormoria's two foundational figures' lineages.**
- **His Marshadow ace is the *direct inheritance* from Roma's original Marshadow bargain** — the centuries-old generational ace passed through the family Roma founded.
- **His Mirroh Necropolis guardianship is the inheritance from Roma's original Giratina bargain** — the right to guard the Distortion gate was Roma's negotiated covenant with the Renegade Pokemon, passed down to her descendants.
- **He doesn't know any of this.** Across centuries, the knowledge of House Langerin's founding has been lost. **Kimaris bonds with his Marshadow without recognizing that the soothsayer who occasionally visits the royal court is his progenitor.**
- **He bears the most heritage-rich bloodline in modern Cormoria** — and he is utterly unaware of it. This is the cleanest *tragic-irony* in the project. Roma watches her bloodline continue without recognition; the bloodline continues without recognizing her.

`[OPEN]` Whether Kimaris ever learns the truth of his heritage during the story (the cleanest design is **no** — preserved as a secret known to Roma, Lethys, and the player who reads the Book of the Moon; Kimaris remains in dignified ignorance)

**Marshadow's late-game deployment — the Necropolis Assault as the unified climactic operation `[LOCKED v0.9.4]`:**

The climactic late-game event that forces Kimaris to deploy Marshadow is **the Sword Cult's all-out attack on the Mirroh Necropolis** — the cult's final operation to seize the Distortion gate as Chien-Pao's Leyline-resonance incarnation point.

**Context: Baradus's late-game discovery `[LOCKED v0.9.4]`:**

Throughout most of the story, the Sword Cult has operated from a *hidden HQ* — location never specified, never visited by the player. The cult has been *searching* for Chien-Pao's Leyline incarnation point (Section 8 — Cult Cosmological Framework). At some point in late Act V or early Act VI, **Baradus discovers** that the Distortion gate to Giratina is guarded in the deepest parts of the Mirroh Necropolis grave. He makes the contextual connection: *this Distortion gate must be Chien-Pao's Leyline point.* He pivots the entire cult operation toward seizing this gate.

`[OPEN]` How exactly Baradus discovers the Necropolis gate's existence — possibly through Silas Moray's Vizier-of-Commerce intelligence network indirectly leaking the knowledge (completing Silas's tragic role as the unknowing enabler); possibly through other channels.

**The Necropolis Assault — the climactic operation:**

This becomes Act VI's central operation — *the* climactic late-game beat:
- **Kimaris and House Langerin defend** the Necropolis with their full force — Marshadow deployed, House retainers, possibly multi-house defensive convergence (Brie Moray with Domdaniel, Templar Arceus order operatives, etc.)
- **The player joins the defense** as the central playable beat of Act VI
- **The Sword Cult brings substantial force** to penetrate the defenses and reach the gate
- **Baradus has brought Nemo to the Necropolis** for the binding ritual — *Nemo's death and Ting-Lu's pass to Osrid happen at the Necropolis itself*, not at a separate HQ
- **The 7v9 final battle happens at the Distortion gate chamber** — Baradus's full Stage 1 team and then Stage 2 team (with the four Treasures + Guzzlord) face the player + Ting-Lu in the deepest part of the Necropolis
- See Section 10 — Act VI for the full unified climax structure

**Combat design implications:**

This is **the largest team-fight set-piece in the project outside the 7v9 final battle itself** — and the 7v9 takes place *during* this same operation. The Necropolis Assault is therefore Act VI's *master scripting task* — a multi-stage scripted battle sequence covering Necropolis defense, deeper penetration, Nemo's death, Ting-Lu's pass, the 7v9 climactic battle, and the sealing ritual.

The Marshadow combat profile becomes important for this set-piece to deliver narratively:
- Marshadow must be *visibly powerful* in a way the player witnesses
- As Kimaris's generational ace at level 100 fighting alongside the player, Marshadow should be the *clear apex predator* of the scene
- ~~`[OPEN]` Marshadow's specific kit~~ — **RESOLVED v0.9.9**: Technician · Life Orb · **Spectral Thief / Shadow Sneak / Close Combat / Bulk Up**.

**Thematic resonance:** When Marshadow deploys, **the Pokemon that slips between underworlds is defending the threshold between worlds.** The lore-resonance is perfect. House Langerin's centuries-long guardianship of the Distortion gate is vindicated in this single defensive action.

**Kimaris's "true team" post-game side quest `[LOCKED v0.9.8]`:**

The Trial 1 team (Crowley + 5 supporting Ghosts at cap 18) is *not* Kimaris's actual best play — it is a teaching fight calibrated for the early-game player. Kimaris's **true team**, led by **Marshadow** as the family's generational ace, is locked as a **post-Champion final-act side quest fight.** This is an *above-cap* peer-tier encounter (level **~L100 `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`** — Marshadow at canonical Mythical-tier strength) — comparable to Sable Ashland's late-game peer-tier Shiny Charm side quest (Section 7 — Sable, locked v0.9.8). **The post-game side quest is the player's opportunity to face Kimaris at his real strength** — the man who tied Mordred 8 years pre-game, deploying the Pokemon he held back from every Trial fight in his career. The full Reserve-Champion roster is locked below `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`. The Trial 1 team's stall-and-Curse strategy is *not* representative of how Kimaris would actually fight at full strength; the side quest is where the player sees what Reserve-Champion-tier Ghost mastery actually looks like.

**The Reserve-Champion roster `[LOCKED v0.9.9]`** (~L100, Marshadow-led — his actual best play and the deliberate anti-thesis of the Trial-1 stall: fast, trapping, overwhelming, anti-attrition):

| Pokémon | Type | Ability | Item | Moves | Role / register |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Marshadow** | Ghost/Fighting | Technician | Life Orb | Spectral Thief / Shadow Sneak / Close Combat / Bulk Up | The ace — the **soul-thief**; Spectral Thief steals the player's stat boosts, then strikes |
| **Gengar (Mega)** | Ghost/Poison | Shadow Tag | Gengarite | Shadow Ball / Sludge Wave / Nasty Plot / Destiny Bond | The **soul-binder** — Shadow Tag denies escape; Destiny Bond takes you down with it. (The grown form of his Trial-1 Gastly) |
| **Dragapult** | Dragon/Ghost | Infiltrator | Choice Specs | Draco Meteor / Shadow Ball / Flamethrower / U-turn | The **speed reveal** — Champion-tier pressure the teaching fight never hinted at |

| **Gholdengo** | Steel/Ghost | Good as Gold | Air Balloon | Make It Rain / Shadow Ball / Nasty Plot / Recover | The **soul beyond affliction** — immune to all status; Steel patches Fairy |
| **Houndstone** | Ghost | Fluffy | Leftovers | Last Respects / Shadow Sneak / Body Press / Play Rough | The **grave-guardian** — Last Respects grows for every fallen ally, so the keeper of the Necropolis dead only strengthens as his legion falls |

- **The reveal:** the Trial-1 team was slow Curse-stall (Eviolite babies, Shedinja's Wonder-Guard gate). This is the opposite — fast, trapping (Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag), and *anti-attrition* (Houndstone punishes grinding his team down). The gentle man who baby-talks a Spiritomb commands a Reserve-Champion machine; that gap is the point.
- **Soul register:** every member is death-coded — soul-thief, soul-binder, soul-commander, disguised soul, unafflicted soul, grave-guardian — the exorcist-sorcerer's spiritual register rendered as a roster.
- **Coverage:** the mono-Ghost Dark weakness is answered by Mimikyu (Fairy) and Marshadow (Fighting); the team wins on speed, trapping, and snowball rather than the Trial-1 stall.
